An Extension of the Kazhdan–Lusztig Equivalence
Lin Chen, Yuchen Fu

Abstract
We prove a tamely ramified version of the Kazhdan–Lusztig equivalence using factorization algebras. More precisely, we establish an equivalence between the DG category of Iwahori–integrable affine Lie algebra representations and the DG category of representations of the “mixed” quantum group. This confirms a conjecture by D. Gaitsgory in [ Gai21 ] .



1
Introduction

1.1
What is Done in This Paper

One of the most beautiful and perhaps unexpected discoveries of representation theory in the 1980s was the link between affine Lie algebras and quantum groups. Let us briefly recall the story.

Let
\displaystyle G
be a reductive group over
\displaystyle\mathbb{C}
, and
\displaystyle\mathfrak{g}
its Lie algebra. There are two ways one can
deform
the category
\displaystyle\Rep(G)
:

•

On one hand, we have the abelian category
\displaystyle(\hat{\mathfrak{g}}_{-\kappa}\operatorname{-mod}^{\mathcal{L}^{+}G})^{\heartsuit}
of smooth representations of
\displaystyle\hat{\mathfrak{g}}_{-\kappa}
which are integrable with respect to the arc group
\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{+}G
. Here
\displaystyle-\kappa
is an invariant symmetric bilinear form on the weight lattice, and
\displaystyle\hat{\mathfrak{g}}_{-\kappa}
is the corresponding affine Lie algebra. We shall denote this category by
\displaystyle\textnormal{KL}_{-\kappa}(G)^{\heartsuit}
;

•

On the other hand, we have
\displaystyle\Rep_{q^{-1}}(G)^{\heartsuit}
, the abelian category of representations of the Lusztig quantum group
\displaystyle U^{\textnormal{Lus}}_{q^{-1}}(G)
at level
1
1

1

Our convention in this paper is that
\displaystyle\kappa
will always correspond to
\displaystyle q
, and
\displaystyle-\kappa
always to
\displaystyle q^{-1}
.

\displaystyle q^{-1}
, which is a
\displaystyle\mathbb{C}^{\times}
-valued quadratic form on the weight lattice.

In a sequence of celebrated papers, Kazhdan and Lusztig
[
KL93
,
KL93a
,
KL94
,
KL94a
,
Lus94
]
proved:

Theorem 1.1.1
.

Let
\displaystyle-\kappa
be either an
irrational
or
negative rational
level, avoiding small roots of unity. Then there exists a
braided monoidal
equivalence:

\textnormal{KL}_{-\kappa}(G)^{\heartsuit}\simeq\textnormal{Rep}_{q^{-1}}(G)^{\heartsuit}.

The situation is most interesting when the level is negative rational, at which the category captures the behavior of the modular representation theory of
\displaystyle G
up to the first Frobenius kernel (c.f.
[
AJS94
]
).

In
[
Gai21
]
, Gaitsgory proposed an extension of the above equivalence to a class with weaker integrability conditions:

•

Let
\displaystyle I\subseteq\mathcal{L}^{+}G
denote the Iwahori subgroup of
\displaystyle\mathcal{L}G
. We also have
\displaystyle\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{I}
, the
renormalized
derived category of Iwahori-integrable smooth representations of
\displaystyle\hat{\mathfrak{g}}
. This category usually goes under the name “integral block of the affine BGG category
\displaystyle\mathcal{O}
”;

•

There is a “mixed” quantum group
\displaystyle U_{q}^{\textnormal{mxd}}(G)
, which a graded Hopf algebra that is Lusztig’s quantum group on the
\displaystyle\mathfrak{n}^{+}
part, and Kac-De Concini quantum group on the
\displaystyle\mathfrak{n}^{-}
part. We let
\displaystyle\textnormal{Rep}_{q}^{\textnormal{mxd}}(G)
denote the
renormalized
derived category of graded representations of
\displaystyle U_{q}^{\textnormal{mxd}}(G)
(see Section
2.7
for precise definitions).

The proposed extension, which we prove in this paper, is that

Theorem 1.1.2

(Main Theorem)
.

Let
\displaystyle\kappa
be a non-critical level avoiding small roots of unity, then there exists an equivalence of DG categories

\mathtt{F}_{\kappa}:\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{I}\simeq\textnormal{Rep}_{q}^{\textnormal{mxd}}(G).

The precise definition of “avoiding small roots of unity” is given in as follows:

Condition 1.1.3
.

For every simple factor
\displaystyle\mathfrak{g}_{i}
of
\displaystyle\mathfrak{g}
, we have
\displaystyle\kappa|_{\mathfrak{g}_{i}}=\frac{c_{i}-h_{i}^{\vee}}{2h_{i}^{\vee}}\textnormal{Kil}_{\mathfrak{g}_{i}}
for some
\displaystyle c_{i}\in\mathbb{C}
, where
\displaystyle\textnormal{Kil}_{\mathfrak{g}_{i}}
is the Killing form on
\displaystyle\mathfrak{g}_{i}
,
\displaystyle h_{i}^{\vee}
is the dual Coxeter number. Let
\displaystyle h_{i}
denote the Coxeter number of this simple factor, and
\displaystyle d_{i}
its lacing number. We say
\displaystyle\kappa

avoids small roots of unity
if each
\displaystyle c_{i}
satisfies the following condition, which is the combination of Definition
8.2.6
and Convention
2.7.1
:

Either
\displaystyle c\not\in\mathbb{Q}
, or
\displaystyle c=\frac{p}{q}
for
\displaystyle(p,q)=1
, such that

\begin{cases}p\geq\max(d_{i}+1,h_{i}-1)&\textnormal{if}~(q,d_{i})=1\\
p\geq\max(d_{i}+1,h_{i}^{\vee}-1)&\textnormal{else}\end{cases}

More explicitly, we have the following table of conditions on the minimal value of
\displaystyle p
required for the equivalence to hold, in comparison with that required by Kazhdan and Lusztig:

Several remarks are in order:

•

Our proof is independent of the original proof by Kazhdan and Lusztig (in fact, we do not yet know that it agrees with the original equivalence: see Expectation
1.2.13
below);

•

The equivalence in Theorem
1.1.2
is not
\displaystyle t
-exact on any rational level;

•

The RHS of the equivalence possesses a braided monoidal structure, hence the category
\displaystyle\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{I}
also admits a braided monoidal structure. To the best of our knowledge, this is not previously known. Because of the non-
\displaystyle t
-exactness of our equivalence, this structure is not easy to describe, and it is highly desirable to have a more concrete understanding of this structure. One potential way of doing this is by considering the
semi-infinite
version of the LHS instead (c.f. Expectation
1.4.3
below);

•

The equivalence in Theorem
1.1.2
is expected to satisfy a number of compatibilities and extensions. However, some technical necessities are still undergoing construction. We hope to realize some of the expectations listed below in subsequent articles.

1.2
Proof via Factorization Algebras

Now we give an overview of our proof strategy.

The basic idea lies in the following categorical pattern. Suppose we have a lax monoidal functor
\displaystyle F:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
between two monoidal categories, then
\displaystyle F
automatically factors as

\mathcal{C}\simeq\textbf{1}_{\mathcal{C}}\operatorname{-mod}(\mathcal{C})\xrightarrow{F^{\textnormal{enh}}}F(\textbf{1})\operatorname{-mod}(\mathcal{D})\xrightarrow{\oblv}\mathcal{D}

where
\displaystyle\textbf{1}_{\mathcal{C}}
is the monoidal unit. Often,
\displaystyle F^{\textnormal{enh}}
has a better chance of being an equivalence than
\displaystyle F
does. Similarly, if
\displaystyle\mathcal{M}
is a
\displaystyle\mathcal{C}
-module category, and
\displaystyle\mathcal{N}
a
\displaystyle\mathcal{D}
-module category, then a functor
\displaystyle F_{\textnormal{Mod}}
compatible with these module structures would upgrade to a functor

\mathcal{M}\simeq\textbf{1}_{\mathcal{C}}\operatorname{-mod}(\mathcal{M})\xrightarrow{F_{\textnormal{Mod}}^{\textnormal{enh}}}F(\textbf{1}_{\mathcal{C}})\operatorname{-mod}(\mathcal{N})\xrightarrow{\oblv}\mathcal{N}

In fact, looking at Theorem
1.1.1
, we have even more data: both sides are
braided monoidal
categories. Since we work with DG categories, we should use the homotopical analogue of “braided monoidal”, i.e. the little 2-disk operad (a.k.a.
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{2}
operad). So, one could hope that there are some
lax
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{2}
functors that translate our categories into categories of
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{2}
-modules over the image of
1
, then hope that these images are amenable to explicit identification.

First problem arises:
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{2}
, being a purely topological notion, interacts poorly with algebraic geometry and Lie theory. But not all hope is lost: it turns out we do have an algebro-geometric analogue of
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{2}
-structures, known as
factorization structure
.

Intuitively, given a smooth complex curve
\displaystyle X
, a factorization structure on an object
\displaystyle\mathcal{C}
(an algebra, a space, a category, etc.) is a sheaf of such objects over the moduli space of finite subsets of
\displaystyle X
, such that its fiber over any
\displaystyle k
-tuple of disjoint points
\displaystyle(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})
is
\displaystyle\mathcal{C}^{\tensor k}
. The behavior of fibers as we move from two disjoint points to a single point then encodes a structure similar to the monoidal structure of an
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{2}
-category.

A slightly more rigorous definition is as follows.
Let
\displaystyle{\mathsf{Comm}_{\textnormal{nu}}}
denote the category of non-empty finite sets and surjective morphisms.
When we describe an object or structure (a prestack, a sheaf, etc)
\displaystyle A
as
factorizable
, such an object or structure will live over the
Ran space
(the space of all finite subsets of our curve
\displaystyle X
) and will satisfy the
factorization property
of being multiplicative on the disjoint locus. For instance, a factorizable D-module is the following data:

•

For each
\displaystyle I\in{\mathsf{Comm}_{\textnormal{nu}}}
, a D-module
\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{I}\in\textnormal{DMod}(X^{I})
;

•

For any map
\displaystyle J\surj I
and the resulting diagonal embedding
\displaystyle\Delta_{IJ}:X^{I}\to X^{J}
, an isomorphism

\Delta_{IJ}^{!}(\mathcal{F}_{J})\simeq\mathcal{F}_{I};

•

Define
\displaystyle(X^{I}\times X^{J})_{\textnormal{disj}}
as the open subscheme of
\displaystyle X^{I}\times X^{J}
whose
\displaystyle S
-point is the subset of
\displaystyle(X^{I}\times X^{J})(S)
that are
disjoint
pairs of points on
\displaystyle X(S)
. For any
\displaystyle I
and
\displaystyle J
, the data also includes an isomorphism

j^{!}(\mathcal{F}_{I}\boxtimes\mathcal{F}_{J})\simeq u^{!}(\mathcal{F}_{I\sqcup J}),

where
\displaystyle j:(X^{I}\times X^{J})_{\textnormal{disj}}\inj X^{I}\times X^{J}
is the embedding of the disjoint locus, and
\displaystyle u:(X^{I}\times X^{J})_{\textnormal{disj}}\to X^{I\sqcup J}
is the union map;

•

As well as all higher homotopy data.

The basic observation is that this description also makes sense for constructible sheaves. And, in the topological world, a fundamental result of Lurie tells us that
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{2}
-structures are equivalent to
topological
factorization structures.
So this brings us to our basic plan of attack:

\displaystyle\textstyle{\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}^{I}_{\kappa}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{\Rep_{q}^{\textnormal{mxd}}(G)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{\mathbb{E}_{2}\textnormal{-Module}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
Higher Algebra
Algebraic Factorization Module
Riemann-Hilbert
Topological Factorization Module

The Betti Side

Let us first look at RHS, where the above intuition holds almost literally. Let
\displaystyle\Rep_{q}(T)
denote the representation category for the quantum torus. There exists an
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{2}
-algebra
\displaystyle\Omega_{q}^{\textnormal{Lus}}

internal to
the braided monoidal category
\displaystyle\textnormal{Rep}_{q}(T)
, which can be obtained by taking Koszul dual of the Kac-De Concini quantum Hopf algebra
\displaystyle U_{q}^{\textnormal{KD}}(N^{-})
. We will establish a non-commutative version of result from
[
BFN10
]
and
[
Fra13
]
which says that

Theorem 1.2.1

(Proposition
12.1.17
)
.

We have an equivalence

\textnormal{Rep}_{q}^{\textnormal{mxd}}(G)\simeq\Omega_{q}^{\textnormal{Lus}}\operatorname{-mod}^{\mathbb{E}_{2}}(\textnormal{Rep}_{q}(T))

for all values of
\displaystyle q
.

Remark 1.2.2
.

In some sense, we skipped a step: we directly matched mixed quantum groups with
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{2}
-modules without saying what the lax
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{2}
functor involved is. Though we do not need this for the present paper, let us note that it is given by cohomology with respect to the Lusztig algebra
\displaystyle U_{q}^{\textnormal{Lus}}(N)
.

An important caveat arises: the category that holds
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{2}
-modules is now
\displaystyle\Rep_{q}(T)
, which is itself only an
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{2}
-category
. Lurie established in
[
Lur12
]
that to each
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{2}
-category one can attach a factorizable
cosheaf
of categories; as we mentioned before, however, our desired notion of factorization category is a
sheaf
. Since Verdier duality does not exist in the unstable setting, we will need to establish a
categorical Verdier duality
to the following effect:

Theorem 1.2.3

(Proposition
6.3.3
, Proposition
6.3.8
)
.

To each
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{2}
DG category
\displaystyle\mathcal{C}
one can attach a topological factorization category
\displaystyle\textnormal{Fact}(\mathcal{C})
, such that the category of (non-unital)
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{2}
-algebras (resp. modules) in
\displaystyle\mathcal{C}
correspond precisely to the category of factorization algebras (resp. modules).

We further show (Corollary
7.2.3
) that

\textnormal{Fact}(\Rep_{q}(T))\simeq\textnormal{Shv}_{\check{\kappa}}(\textnormal{Gr}_{\check{T}}(\mathbb{C}))

here
\displaystyle\textnormal{Shv}_{\check{\kappa}}
denote the category of
Vect
-valued topological sheaves (twisted by a certain gerbe), and
\displaystyle\textnormal{Gr}_{\check{T}}
is the
affine Grassmannian
.

Corollary 1.2.4
.

There exists an equivalence of categories

\textnormal{FAlg}:\mathbb{E}_{2}\textnormal{-Alg}_{\textnormal{nu}}(\Rep_{q}(T))\to\textnormal{FactAlg}(\textnormal{Shv}_{\check{\kappa}}(\textnormal{Gr}_{\check{T}}(\mathbb{C})))

(here
nu
indicates non-unitality), and, for every non-unital
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{2}
-algebra
\displaystyle A
in
\displaystyle\Rep_{q}(T)
, an equivalence of categories

\textnormal{FMod}:A\operatorname{-mod}^{\mathbb{E}_{2}}(\Rep_{q}(T))\simeq\textnormal{FAlg}(A)\textnormal{-FactMod}(\textnormal{Shv}_{\check{\kappa}}(\textnormal{Gr}_{\check{T}}(\mathbb{C}))).

Remark 1.2.5
.

Since the pioneering work of
[
FS94
]
,
[
BFS06
]
it has been known that quantum groups (and more generally, sufficiently small Hopf algebras) and their representations can be encoded with topological factorization data. Because we work with derived objects, we opt to use the Koszul dual description of
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{2}
-algebras. In particular, our proof method is independent of
[
BFS06
]
.

The de Rham Side

Now we look at Kac-Moody representations. First we have to answer the question: who is our acting category
\displaystyle\mathcal{C}
? The initial guess would be
\displaystyle\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{I}
itself, but this turns out to be not quite right, because
\displaystyle I
as a group scheme
does not factorize
; intuitively, this means this category doesn’t know how to move around on the curve (see, however, Expectation
1.4.3
).

On the other hand,
\displaystyle\textnormal{KL}_{\kappa}(G)
, the derived version of
\displaystyle\textnormal{KL}_{\kappa}(G)^{\heartsuit}
, does. Indeed, we will show that
\displaystyle\textnormal{KL}_{\kappa}(G)
admits an enhancement as a
factorization category
, and
\displaystyle\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{I}
is a
factorization module category
over
\displaystyle\textnormal{KL}_{\kappa}(G)
. This should be considered as encoding the fact that
\displaystyle\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{I}
is a module over
\displaystyle\textnormal{KL}_{\kappa}(G)
under the Kazhdan–Lusztig fusion tensor product, an observation tracing back to
[
Fin93
]
.

Let us look at our intuition again. Note that, in the very first step we used the (almost tautological) equivalence of
\displaystyle\mathcal{M}\simeq\textbf{1}_{\mathcal{C}}\operatorname{-mod}(\mathcal{M})
. It is, however, less obvious how to make sense of this step in algebraic geometry.

The additional input is that of a
unital factorization structure
. In the same D-module example, this is following
additional data
:

•

For every
injective map

\displaystyle p:I\inj J
and the corresponding projection
\displaystyle\pi_{p}:X^{J}\to X^{I}
, a map

\pi_{p}^{!}(A_{I})\to A_{J}

in a way compatible with all of the data above;

•

Additionally, we also allow
\displaystyle I
to be
\displaystyle\emptyset
now. This gives, in particular, a map of factorization algebras
\displaystyle\omega_{\textnormal{Ran}}\to\mathcal{F}
. The object coming from
\displaystyle I=\emptyset
will be called the
vacuum
;

Example 1.2.6
.

In the case of the Kazhdan–Lusztig category, the vacuum is precisely the Kac-Moody vacuum vertex algebra
\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{\mathfrak{g},\kappa}
, considered as an element of
\displaystyle\textnormal{KL}_{\kappa}(G)
.

Remark 1.2.7
.

We emphasize that the unital structure
fundamentally
alters the behavior of the categories involved. One may intuitively think of this as due to the fact that the unital Ran space has very different topology from the non-unital one.

Using
factorizable renormalized ind-coherent sheaves
(this is a new technical tool we introduce), we will show that category
\displaystyle\textnormal{KL}_{\kappa}(G)
is indeed an
unital
factorization category, carrying
\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{\mathfrak{g},\kappa}
as its vacuum. The unital structure, intuitively speaking, encodes how these vacuum modules can appear at all places and how they can interact with our given Kac-Moody representation (considered as fixed at a point on the curve).

Next we want to find a candidate for
\displaystyle F_{\textnormal{Mod}}
. A crucial observation, made at the abelian level by Beilinson and Drinfeld in
[
BDD04
, Chapter 3.8]
, is that
\displaystyle C_{*}^{\frac{\infty}{2}}(\mathcal{L}\mathfrak{n},-)
, the
semi-infinite cohomology
functor (introduced by
[
Fei84
]
) with respect to the nilpotent subalgebra
\displaystyle\mathcal{L}\mathfrak{n}
, is a
factorizable
functor. Let
\displaystyle\textnormal{KL}_{\kappa^{\prime}}(T)
denote the Kazhdan–Lusztig category for the torus, the general theory of
unital factorization categories
then upgrades the functor

C_{*}^{\frac{\infty}{2}}(\mathcal{L}\mathfrak{n},-):\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{I}\to\textnormal{KL}_{\kappa^{\prime}}(T)

to a functor

C_{*}^{\frac{\infty}{2}}(\mathcal{L}\mathfrak{n},-)^{\textnormal{enh}}:\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{I}\to C_{*}^{\frac{\infty}{2}}(\mathcal{L}\mathfrak{n},\mathbb{V}^{0}_{\kappa})\textnormal{-FactMod}(\textnormal{KL}_{\kappa^{\prime}}(T))

where RHS is the category of factorization modules over the
factorization algebra

\displaystyle C_{*}^{\frac{\infty}{2}}(\mathcal{L}\mathfrak{n},\mathbb{V}^{0}_{\kappa})
. Here
\displaystyle\kappa^{\prime}
denotes the
shifted level
that semi-infinite cohomology maps into.

To produce actual sheaves, we will need to prove the following folklore:

Proposition 1.2.8

(Proposition
5.3.4
, “Toric FLE”)
.

There exists an equivalence of unital factorization categories

\textnormal{FLE}_{T}:\textnormal{KL}_{\kappa^{\prime}}(T)\simeq\textnormal{DMod}_{\check{\kappa}^{\prime}}(\textnormal{Gr}_{\check{T}}).

Let us set
\displaystyle\Omega_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}:=\textnormal{FLE}_{T}\circ C_{*}^{\frac{\infty}{2}}(\mathcal{L}\mathfrak{n},\mathbb{V}^{0}_{\kappa})
, so we can define

J_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}:=\textnormal{FLE}_{T}\circ C_{*}^{\frac{\infty}{2}}(\mathcal{L}\mathfrak{n},-)^{\textnormal{enh}}:\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{I}\to\Omega_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}\textnormal{-FactMod}(\textnormal{DMod}_{\check{\kappa}^{\prime}}(\textnormal{Gr}_{\check{T}}))

Our main result is that

Theorem 1.2.9

(Theorem
2.6.3
)
.

At positive (or irrational) levels,
\displaystyle J_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}
is an equivalence of categories.

We emphasize that this equivalence
only
holds for positive levels.

Remark 1.2.10
.

The appearance of semi-infinite cohomology deserves some explanation. The category
\displaystyle\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}
is a category with a strong
\displaystyle\mathcal{L}G
action, and our category
\displaystyle\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{I}
is its
\displaystyle I
-invariant category. Now,
[
Ras16
, Section 6.2.1]
showed that for any category
\displaystyle\mathcal{C}
with a strong
\displaystyle\mathcal{L}G
-action, we have equivalence of categories

\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{L}N\mathcal{L}^{+}T}\simeq\mathcal{C}_{I}\simeq\mathcal{C}^{I}\simeq\mathcal{C}^{\mathcal{L}N\mathcal{L}^{+}T},

here superscript (resp. subscript) denotes invariant (resp. coinvariant). Therefore, the
affine
category
\displaystyle\mathcal{O}
coincides with the coinvariant
3
3

3

The semi-infinite invariance and coinvariance categories both admit factorization structure, but they
do not agree
as factorization categories. For reasons related to local Langlands, we think of the
coinvariance
category as the right choice at positive levels.

semi-infinite
category
\displaystyle\mathcal{O}

\displaystyle(\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa})_{\mathcal{L}N\mathcal{L}^{+}T}
, and the functor
\displaystyle J_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}
should really be thought of as mapping out of the latter.

In order to prove Theorem
1.2.9
, we observe that both sides have the structure of highest-weight categories, and proceed to match standard and costandard objects from both sides. For the same reason as in the previous remark, our choice of standard objects on the LHS will be the (dual objects of)
semi-infinite
Verma modules, also known as Wakimoto modules.

It is not easy, however, to directly show that standard objects go to standard objects: in the setting of factorization modules, the standard objects are characterized by having simple
\displaystyle*
-fibers, which we have very little control of in general. To handle this
\displaystyle*
-fiber, we will establish a non-trivial
local-global compatibility
, which is the following diagram (we use a slight variant in the actual proof):

\displaystyle\textstyle{\textnormal{KL}_{\kappa}(G)_{x}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\scriptstyle{C_{*}^{\frac{\infty}{2}}(\mathcal{L}\mathfrak{n},-)}
\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\textnormal{Loc}_{x}}
\displaystyle\textstyle{C_{*}^{\frac{\infty}{2}}(\mathcal{L}\mathfrak{n},\mathbb{V}_{\kappa}^{0})\textnormal{-FactMod}(\textnormal{KL}_{\kappa^{\prime}}(T)_{x})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\textnormal{Loc}^{\textnormal{ch}}_{x}}
\displaystyle\textstyle{\textnormal{DMod}_{\kappa}(\textnormal{Bun}_{G}(\mathbb{P}^{1}))\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\textnormal{CT}_{*}[-d]}
\displaystyle\textstyle{\textnormal{DMod}_{\kappa^{\prime}}(\textnormal{Bun}_{T}(\mathbb{P}^{1}))}

here we consider
\displaystyle x
as a fixed point on
\displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{1}
, so that LHS can be seen as the usual localization procedure from Kac-Moody representation to D-modules on
\displaystyle\textnormal{Bun}_{G}
. The RHS is
chiral localization
, which roughly means doing localization at every point
at the same time
, with the vacuum
\displaystyle C_{*}^{\frac{\infty}{2}}(\mathcal{L}\mathfrak{n},\mathbb{V}_{\kappa}^{0})
filling in every other point on the curve. Finally,
\displaystyle\textnormal{CT}_{*}
is the
geometric constant term functor
, and
\displaystyle d
is a cohomological shift. This allows us to relate the
\displaystyle*
-fibers to
conformal blocks
, from which the result follows.

\displaystyle\textstyle{\textnormal{Algebraic}~\Omega_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}\textnormal{-Factorization Module}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
Riemann-Hilbert
\displaystyle\textstyle{\textnormal{Topological}~\textnormal{FAlg}(\Omega^{\textnormal{Lus}}_{q})\textnormal{-Factorization Module}}

To link the two worlds, we show that

Proposition 1.2.11

(Corollary
13.3.1
, Corollary
13.3.6
)
.

There exists a factorizable system of equivalence of categories

\textnormal{RH}:\textnormal{DMod}_{\check{\kappa}^{\prime}}(\textnormal{Gr}_{\check{T}})\simeq\textnormal{Shv}_{\check{\kappa}^{\prime}}(\textnormal{Gr}_{\check{T}}(\mathbb{C})).

The functor
RH
preserves factorization algebras, and, for every factorization algebra
\displaystyle A
, induces an equivalence of categories

A\textnormal{-FactMod}(\textnormal{KL}_{\kappa^{\prime}}(T))\simeq\textnormal{RH}(A)\textnormal{-FactMod}(\textnormal{Shv}_{\check{\kappa}^{\prime}}(\textnormal{Gr}_{\check{T}}(\mathbb{C}))).

The last ingredient of the proof is that

Proposition 1.2.12

(Proposition
2.9.5
)
.

For
\displaystyle\kappa
positive and avoiding small roots of unity, we have

\textnormal{RH}(\Omega_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa})\simeq\textnormal{FAlg}(\Omega^{\textnormal{Lus}}_{q}).

The proof of this statement relies on the fact that our factorization algebra is in fact a
perverse sheave
that admit a combinatorial description (obtained in
[
Gai21a
]
), so that to match the two sides it suffices to compute their
\displaystyle!
- and
\displaystyle*
- fibers up to some low cohomological degrees.

Then, Theorem
1.2.9
, Theorem
1.2.1
, Corollary
1.2.4
, Proposition
1.2.11
and Proposition
1.2.12
together imply Theorem
1.1.2
when
\displaystyle\kappa
is positive (or irrational).

Negative Levels

For every DG category
\displaystyle\mathcal{C}
, we have its dual category
\displaystyle\mathcal{C}^{\vee}:=\textnormal{Fun}_{\textnormal{cont}}(\mathcal{C},\textnormal{Vect})
consisting of colimit-preserving functors from
\displaystyle\mathcal{C}
to
Vect
. On the Kac-Moody side, we have a
categorical
(a.k.a. cohomological) duality (c.f. Definition
2.3.5
):

\hat{\mathfrak{g}}_{-\kappa}\operatorname{-mod}^{I}\simeq(\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{I})^{\vee}

On the quantum side, we have the
contragredient duality
(c.f. Definition
2.8.9
):

\Rep^{\textnormal{mxd}}_{q^{-1}}(G)\simeq(\Rep^{\textnormal{mxd}}_{q}(G))^{\vee}.

Thus for
\displaystyle-\kappa
negative, there also exists an equivalence of categories

\mathtt{F}_{-\kappa}:\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{-\kappa}^{I}\xrightarrow{\simeq}\textnormal{Rep}_{q^{-1}}^{\textnormal{mxd}}(G)

defined as the
dual functor
of
\displaystyle\mathtt{F}_{\kappa}
.

As mentioned in the beginning, it is an important — and non-trivial — question whether our equivalence agrees with that of Kazhdan and Lusztig.

Expectation 1.2.13
.

We expect that
\displaystyle\mathtt{F}_{-\kappa}
induces a
\displaystyle t
-exact equivalence on the
\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{+}G
-invariant category at the negative level, which is the functor in Theorem
1.1.1
.

Remark 1.2.14
.

The Jacquet functor
\displaystyle J_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}
described in this paper exists for negative levels, but is
not
an equivalence there.

1.3
Technical Aspects

The bulk of the present paper’s content is
theory-building
: indeed, once all the tools have been set up, it takes only a few pages’ calculation to get to the desired result. So here we make a list of main technical aspects that constitute the backbone of this work, and offer some perspectives on their necessity:

1.

We further extended Raskin’s theory of
renormalized ind-coherent sheaves
(
[
Ras20a
]
) to provide it with extra functoriality and more base-change. Other than being of independent algebro-geometric interest, we emphasize that this is what makes everything work (factorizability of semi-infinite cohomology and local-global comparison, among other things);

2.

As far as we are aware of, the present work produces the first instance of a
factorizable system of ind-coherent sheaves
. Let us emphasize that even the plausibility of such an object is not a priori obvious, because ind-coherent sheaves do not form a sheaf of categories: indeed, only after renormalizing
4
4

4

We note this is a different renormalization from the one on Kac-Moody representations.
the presheaf of categories do we obtain such a system. We expect this technique to be more widely applicable, for instance in the study of
factorizable weak group actions
;

3.

We fully implemented the
categorical Verdier duality
necessary for converting twisted Hopf algebras into twisted factorizable sheaves. This has been a folklore in the community for over 10 years. We also note that this method is fully homotopic in nature and completely bypasses
5
5

5

On the other hand, one advantage of directly working with Hopf algebras is the ability to stay with the heart of the
\displaystyle t
-structure, which reduces homotopy coherence to a finite level.
the hyperplane arrangement argument in
[
BFS06
]
.

1.4
Additional Remarks

Hecke Equivariance

Recall we have the Iwahori Hecke category
\displaystyle\textnormal{DMod}_{\kappa}(I\backslash\mathcal{L}G/I)
which naturally acts on
\displaystyle\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{I}
via convolution. Using the equivalence we establish, it also acts on
\displaystyle\Rep_{q}^{\textnormal{mxd}}(G)
.

Let
\displaystyle H
be the metaplectic dual of
\displaystyle G
(c.f. Definition
2.3.7
). We have the following metaplectic extension of R. Bezrukavnikov’s result in
[
Bez16
]
to rational levels (work-in-progress of Dhillon, Yun and Zhu):

\textnormal{DMod}_{\kappa}(I\backslash\mathcal{L}G/I)\simeq\textnormal{IndCoh}(\left(\widetilde{\mathcal{N}}_{H}\times_{\mathfrak{h}}\widetilde{\mathcal{N}}_{H}\right)/H)

(Note that the RHS is not quite right: we should have a
singular support condition
on it. Here and below we will momentarily ignore this problem.)

Expectation 1.4.1
.

We expect
\displaystyle\textnormal{IndCoh}(\left(\widetilde{\mathcal{N}}_{H}\times_{\mathfrak{h}}\widetilde{\mathcal{N}}_{H}\right)/H)
to act naturally on
\displaystyle\Rep_{q}^{\textnormal{mxd}}(G)
, and that
\displaystyle\mathsf{F}_{\kappa}
is equivariant with respect to this action via the equivalence above.

Remark 1.4.2
.

In
[
Gai21
, Section 7.2.3]
Gaitsgory conjectured an action of
\displaystyle\textnormal{QCoh}(\mathfrak{n}_{H}/B_{H})
on
\displaystyle\Rep_{q}^{\textnormal{mxd}}(G)_{\textnormal{ren}}
. Within the paradigm above it would be provided by the map

\textnormal{QCoh}(\mathfrak{n}_{H}/B_{H})\xrightarrow{\Upsilon}\textnormal{IndCoh}(\mathfrak{n}_{H}/B_{H})\simeq\textnormal{IndCoh}(\widetilde{\mathcal{N}}_{H}/H)\xrightarrow{\Delta_{*}}\textnormal{IndCoh}(\left(\widetilde{\mathcal{N}}_{H}\times_{\mathfrak{h}}\widetilde{\mathcal{N}}_{H}\right)/H).

A description of this action is now known and will be included in a subsequent article.

Factorizable Equivalence

By
[
Lur12
]
, the category
\displaystyle\Rep_{q}^{\textnormal{mxd}}(G)
is an
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{2}
category itself, so Theorem
1.2.3
allows us to attach to it a topological factorization category
\displaystyle\textnormal{Fact}(\Rep_{q}^{\textnormal{mxd}}(G))
. On the other hand, recall that we have
\displaystyle\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{I}\simeq(\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa})_{\mathcal{L}N\mathcal{L}^{+}T}
and the RHS has an algebraic factorization category structure.
One is thus naturally led to wonder about the existence of a factorizable system of equivalences

\mathtt{F}_{\kappa}^{\textnormal{Fact}}:(\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa})_{\mathcal{L}N\mathcal{L}^{+}T}\simeq\textnormal{Fact}(\Rep_{q}^{\textnormal{mxd}}(G))

that extends the functor
\displaystyle\mathtt{F}_{\kappa}
at a point.

Expectation 1.4.3
.

We expect some version of this equivalence to exist.

1.5
Fundamental Local Equivalence

The result of this paper fits naturally into the local geometric Langlands program, initiated in Frenkel and Gaitsgory in
[
FG06
]
. We briefly summarize the ideas here.

Let
\displaystyle\kappa
denote the quantum parameter (for
\displaystyle G
a simple group it is just an element of
\displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{C})
), and let
\displaystyle\check{\kappa}
denote the Langlands dual parameter. Let
\displaystyle\check{G}
denote the Langlands dual group of
\displaystyle G
. An expected output of the 2-categorical formalism of local geometric Langlands is:

Conjecture 1.5.1

(Spherical Fundamental Local Equivalence (FLE))
.

For any level
\displaystyle\kappa
, We have an equivalence of (unital) factorization categories

\textnormal{KL}_{\kappa}(G)\simeq\textnormal{Whit}(\textnormal{DMod}_{\check{\kappa}}(\textnormal{Gr}_{\check{G}}));

here
\displaystyle\textnormal{KL}_{\kappa}(G)
is as defined above,
\displaystyle\textnormal{Gr}_{\check{G}}
is the affine Grassmannian, and the RHS (known as the spherical Whittaker category) is the strong
\displaystyle\mathcal{L}N
-invariant of
\displaystyle\textnormal{DMod}_{\check{\kappa}}(\textnormal{Gr}_{\check{G}})
with respect to a non-dgenerate character
\displaystyle\chi
,
\displaystyle N
being the unipotent subgroup of a fixed Borel of
\displaystyle G
.

We emphasize that the word “factorization” is what makes the statement most interesting, as being a factorization category is akin to (though inequivalent to) having a braided monoidal structure on the category.

Remark 1.5.2
.

The global geometric Langlands program, which aims to prove the following equivalence of categories

\textnormal{DMod}(\textnormal{Bun}_{G})\simeq^{?}\textnormal{IndCoh}_{\textnormal{Nilp}}(\textnormal{LocSys}_{\check{G}}),

has the following guiding philosophy: the LHS and RHS are respectively fairly close to the factorization homology of
\displaystyle\textnormal{Whit}(\textnormal{DMod}_{\kappa_{\textnormal{crit}}}(\textnormal{Gr}_{G}))
and
\displaystyle\textnormal{KL}_{\infty}(\check{G})\simeq\Rep(\check{G})
over the curve (here
\displaystyle\kappa_{\textnormal{crit}}
is the critical level). Because of this, FLE is considered a central component towards establishing (classical and quantum) global geometric Langlands. For a more precise formulation of the role Conjecture
1.5.1
plays in the global setting, see
[
Gai15
]
.

Remark 1.5.3
.

While the factorizable version of this conjecture remains quite open (except for when
\displaystyle G=T
is a torus, which we establish here in Proposition
5.3.4
), its fiberwise statement (i.e. with the word “factorization” removed) is more tractable. For instance, the cases of
\displaystyle\kappa=\kappa_{\textnormal{crit}}
and
\displaystyle\kappa=\infty
were known by
[
Bez+19
]
and
[
FG09
]
respectively, and at almost all levels this is now known by the work of
[
CDR19
]
via affine Soergel bimodules.

One strategy proposed by Gaitsgory for proving the FLE (factorizably) is by linking both sides to quantum groups:

\displaystyle\textstyle{\textnormal{KL}_{\kappa}(G)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
FLE
\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\simeq}
KL
\displaystyle\textstyle{\textnormal{Whit}(\textnormal{DMod}_{\check{\kappa}}(\textnormal{Gr}_{\check{G}}))}
\displaystyle\textstyle{\textnormal{Rep}_{q}(G)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\simeq}
CS

where on the left we have (a conjectural factorizable version of) the Kazhdan–Lusztig equivalence, and on the right we have the (conjectural)
quantum Casselman-Shalika formula
. It is expected that both (KL) and (CS) can be proven factorizably.

Remark 1.5.4
.

We warn that it is a non-trivial matter to convert the braided monoidal structure of the classical Kazhdan–Lusztig equivalence to a form that is usable for geometric Langlands’ purpose, as the braided monoidal structure there is not local (or even algebraic) by nature.

Instead the logic goes the reverse order: we expect the methods established in the present paper will eventually yield a proof of (KL) as an factorizable equivalence, from which we hope to extract a
new proof
of the Kazhdan–Lusztig braided monoidal equivalence.

For the Iwahori subgroup, the counterpart of FLE is

Proposition 1.5.5

(Iwahori / Tamely Ramified FLE (IFLE))
.

For any level
\displaystyle\kappa
we have an equivalence of categories

\hat{\mathfrak{g}}_{\kappa}\operatorname{-mod}^{I}\simeq\textnormal{Whit}(\textnormal{DMod}_{\check{\kappa}}(\textnormal{Fl}_{\check{G}}));

here
\displaystyle\textnormal{Fl}_{\check{G}}
is the affine Flag variety.

Note that the word “factorization” has disappeared from the formulation, since the Iwahori group does not have a factorizable analogue (see, however, Expectation
1.4.3
above). The corresponding picture involving quantum groups becomes

\displaystyle\textstyle{\hat{\mathfrak{g}}_{\kappa}\operatorname{-mod}^{I}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
IFLE
\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\simeq}
Theorem
1.1.2
\displaystyle\textstyle{\textnormal{Whit}(\textnormal{DMod}_{\check{\kappa}}(\textnormal{Fl}_{\check{G}}))}
\displaystyle\textstyle{\textnormal{Rep}^{\textnormal{mxd}}_{q}(G)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\simeq}
\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\textnormal{CS}_{\textnormal{Fl}}}

where now all arrows are actual theorems: the LHS is the main result of this paper, and RHS can be obtained by combining
[
Yan21
]
with Theorem
1.2.1
, Corollary
1.2.4
and Proposition
1.2.11
.
We note that the top arrow is also independently established in
[
CDR19
]
; however, if we interpret the top arrow as the equivalence in
loc.cit.
, then the commutativity of the triangle is not yet known.

Proof Outline

For reader’s convenience, we will first present the main proof in this section, after stating all of the definitions and background results necessary to process it. Proofs of individual statements can be found in later sections.

2.1
Conventions

Base Field

We will work over
\displaystyle k=\mathbb{C}
. Most results unrelated to Riemann-Hilbert hold true for any algebraically closed field of characteristic
\displaystyle 0
, but we do not need this generality.

Category Theory

We use the theory of
\displaystyle\infty
-categories set up in
[
Lur09
]
. At several points we will make use of the theory of
\displaystyle(\infty,2)
-categories; for some foundational setup, we refer our readers to the appendix of
[
GR17
]
. By a
category
we always mean an
\displaystyle(\infty,1)
-category unless specified otherwise; similarly by a
2-category
we mean an
\displaystyle(\infty,2)
-category. We let

•

Spc
denote the category of
\displaystyle\infty
-groupoids;

•

\displaystyle 1\textnormal{-Cat}
denote the category of all (small)
\displaystyle(\infty,1)
-categories, and
\displaystyle 1\textnormal{-Cat}^{2\textnormal{-Cat}}
denote the enhancement of it into a 2-category;

•

\displaystyle\textnormal{Pr}^{\textnormal{L, St}}
denote the (symmetric monoidal) category of stable, presentable categories and continuous (colimit-preserving) functors;

•

Vect
denote the category of chain complexes of vector spaces over
\displaystyle k
;

•

DGCat
denote the (symmetric monoidal) category
\displaystyle\textnormal{Vect}\operatorname{-mod}(\textnormal{Pr}^{\textnormal{L, St}})
, and
\displaystyle\textnormal{DGCat}_{*}
denote the (symmetric monoidal) category of pairs
\displaystyle(c,\mathcal{C})
, where
\displaystyle\mathcal{C}\in\textnormal{DGCat}
and
\displaystyle c\in\mathcal{C}
.

Higher Algebra

We make frequent use of terminologies and facts about homotopical algebra as set up in
[
Lur12
]
.

Derived Categories

The derived category of an Grothendieck abelian category
\displaystyle\mathcal{A}
for us will refer to the
\displaystyle\infty
-category of
unbounded
chain complexes in
\displaystyle\mathcal{A}
localized with respect to quasi-isomorphisms. We refer readers to
[
Lur12
, Chapter 1]
for a detailed discussion. We adopt the
cohomological
grading convention.

When we write
\displaystyle\Hom(X,Y)
for objects in a DG category, we always mean the entire mapping chain complex; we write
\displaystyle\textnormal{Ext}^{n}
when we want to refer to its
\displaystyle n
th cohomology.

Algebraic Geometry

For foundation of derived algebraic geometry, we refer readers to
[
GR17
]
and
[
Lur18
]
. Our terminologies and conventions will follow that of
[
GR17
]
.

Let
\displaystyle\textnormal{CAlg}^{\leq 0}
be the category of connective commutative algebra objects in
Vect
. We let

•

\displaystyle\textnormal{Sch}^{\textnormal{aff}}:=(\textnormal{CAlg}^{\leq 0})^{\textnormal{op}}
denote the category of affine schemes;

•

PreStk
denote the
\displaystyle(\infty,1)
-category of
Spc
-valued presheaves over
\displaystyle\textnormal{Sch}^{\textnormal{aff}}
;

•

LaxPreStk
denote the
\displaystyle(\infty,2)
-category of
\displaystyle 1\textnormal{-Cat}
-valued presheaves over
\displaystyle\textnormal{Sch}^{\textnormal{aff}}
.

Given a prestack
\displaystyle\mathcal{Y}
, we use
\displaystyle\mathcal{Y}_{\textnormal{dR}}
to denote the de Rham prestack defined by
\displaystyle\mathcal{Y}_{\textnormal{dR}}(S):=\mathcal{Y}(S^{\textnormal{red, cl}})
, where
\displaystyle S^{\textnormal{red, cl}}
is the corresponding classical reduced affine scheme.

Factorization Structure

In the introduction we gave an informal definition of what a factorization structure is; an equivalent (see Section
10
for proof) way of formulating it is as follows.

We consider
\displaystyle\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu},\textnormal{dR}}
, the non-unital
Ran space
of
\displaystyle X_{\textnormal{dR}}
, which is the prestack whose space of
\displaystyle S
-points is the space of finite subsets of
\displaystyle X_{\textnormal{dR}}(S)
.
A non-unital factorization space is then an object
\displaystyle\mathcal{Y}_{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{dR}}}\in\textnormal{PreStk}
over
\displaystyle\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu},\textnormal{dR}}
along with the following extra data: for every point
\displaystyle\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\}\in\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu},\textnormal{dR}}(S)
that lies in the disjoint locus
6
6

6

For
\displaystyle S=\mathbb{C}
the meaning of “disjoint” is clear; for general
\displaystyle S
see Section
10
. For the sake of intuition it does little harm to only consider the case of
\displaystyle\mathbb{C}
-points.
, we require an isomorphism

\mathcal{Y}_{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{dR}}}|_{\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\}}\simeq\mathcal{Y}_{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{dR}}}|_{x_{1}}\times_{S}\mathcal{Y}_{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{dR}}}|_{x_{1}}\times_{S}\ldots\times_{S}\mathcal{Y}_{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{dR}}}|_{x_{n}}.

If one replaces “prestack over
\displaystyle\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu},\textnormal{dR}}
” with “D-modules over
\displaystyle\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu},\textnormal{dR}}
”, one obtains the notion of non-unital factorization
algebras
. If one instead uses “sheaves of categories over
\displaystyle\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu},\textnormal{dR}}
,” one obtains the notion of non-unital factorization
categories
. By considering sheaves of
pointed
categories, one obtains the notion of non-unital factorization algebras
internal
to a factorization category. For a fully rigorous definition, see Section
10
.

Let
\displaystyle x_{0}\in X_{\textnormal{dR}}(\mathbb{C})
be a fixed
\displaystyle\mathbb{C}
-point. Consider
\displaystyle\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu},x_{0},\textnormal{dR}}
, the prestack whose space of
\displaystyle S
-points is the space of finite subsets of
\displaystyle X_{\textnormal{dR}}(S)
containing
\displaystyle S\to\textnormal{Spec}(\mathbb{C})\xrightarrow{x_{0}}X_{\textnormal{dR}}
. Fix a non-unital factorization space
\displaystyle\mathcal{A}
; a non-unital factorization module space is a prestack
\displaystyle\mathcal{Z}
over
\displaystyle\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu},x_{0},\textnormal{dR}}
along with the following extra data: for every
\displaystyle\{x_{0},x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\}\in\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu},x_{0},\textnormal{dR}}(S)
that lies in the disjoint locus, we require an isomorphism

\mathcal{Z}|_{\{x_{0},\ldots,x_{n}\}}\simeq\mathcal{Z}|_{x_{0}}\times_{S}\mathcal{A}|_{x_{1}}\times_{S}\ldots\times_{S}\mathcal{A}|_{x_{n}};

The notion of factorization module categories and (internal) factorization module algebras can be defined analogously; we can also replace
\displaystyle x_{0}
by a finite set of fixed points.

A word on unitality: as we mentioned in the introduction, the notion of unital structure in the factorization setting plays many crucial technical roles; on the other hand, it does render some of the definitions more cumbersome. We thus suggest readers to ignore all things related to unital structure on the first pass by considering it as an analogue of the unital structure in the
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{2}
-world, and refer to the appendix for a rigorous treatment if needs be.

Reductive Group

For
\displaystyle G
a connected reductive group, we write
\displaystyle\mathcal{L}G
(resp.
\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{+}G
) for the prestacks given by

\mathcal{L}G(A):=G(A(\!(t)\!))\hskip 10.00002pt\mathcal{L}^{+}G(A):=G(A[\![t]\!]).

We refer to them as the loop (resp. arc) group of
\displaystyle G
. It is well-known that
\displaystyle\mathcal{L}G
is an indscheme and
\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{+}G
a scheme, albeit both of infinite type. We let
\displaystyle\textnormal{Gr}_{G}
denote the fppf sheaf quotient
\displaystyle\mathcal{L}G/\mathcal{L}^{+}G
.

There are well-known factorizable spaces over
\displaystyle\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{dR}}
, which we’ll denote by

[\mathcal{L}G]_{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{dR}}},[\mathcal{L}^{+}G]_{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{dR}}},[\textnormal{Gr}_{G}]_{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{dR}}}

respectively, whose fiber at any
\displaystyle\mathbb{C}
-point on
\displaystyle X
recovers the prestacks defined above.

We fix a standard Borel
\displaystyle B
and a maximal torus
\displaystyle T
of
\displaystyle G
. We let
\displaystyle N
denote the unipotent part of
\displaystyle B
. We let
\displaystyle B^{-}
and
\displaystyle N^{-}
denote the opposite Borel (resp. unipotent). We let
\displaystyle\mathfrak{g}
(resp.
\displaystyle\mathfrak{b},\mathfrak{n},\mathfrak{t}
) refer to the Lie algebras.

We let
\displaystyle(\check{\Lambda},\check{\Delta},\Lambda,\Delta)
denote the root datum corresponding to
\displaystyle(G,T)
. Here
\displaystyle\Lambda
denote the coweight lattice of
\displaystyle G
,
\displaystyle\check{\Lambda}
its weight lattice,
\displaystyle\Delta
its coroot lattice and
\displaystyle\check{\Delta}
its root lattice.

The superscript
\displaystyle<0
(resp.
\displaystyle\leq 0,>0,\geq 0
) on the (co)weight lattice will always refer to the submonoid generated by negative (resp. non-positive, etc.) (co)
roots
; in other words, the inequality signs refer to the standard Bruhat order. The superscript
\displaystyle+
and
\displaystyle-
will mean
dominant
and
anti-dominant
respectively.

We let
\displaystyle W_{\textnormal{fin}}
denote the finite Weyl group of
\displaystyle(G,T)
,
\displaystyle W_{\textnormal{aff}}
the affine Weyl group, and
\displaystyle W_{\textnormal{aff,ext}}
the extended affine Weyl group of
\displaystyle G
.

We let
\displaystyle I
be the Iwahori subgroup, defined as the preimage of
\displaystyle B
under
\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{+}(G)\xrightarrow{t=0}G
.

Global Structure

Let
\displaystyle X
be a smooth complete algebraic curve over
\displaystyle\mathbb{C}
. For each reductive group
\displaystyle G
, we let
\displaystyle\textnormal{Bun}_{G}(X)
denote the moduli stack of
\displaystyle G
-bundles on
\displaystyle X
; this stack is smooth and classical, of dimension
\displaystyle\dim(\mathfrak{g})(g(X)-1)
, where
\displaystyle g(X)
is the genus of
\displaystyle X
. When
\displaystyle X
is clear from the context, we will denote it simply by
\displaystyle\textnormal{Bun}_{G}
.
We fix
\displaystyle\omega_{X}^{1/2}
, a square root of the canonical bundle on
\displaystyle X
.

Quantum Parameters

A
quantum parameter
(introduced in
[
Zha20
]
) is, by definition, a pair
\displaystyle[\kappa,E]
where
\displaystyle\kappa
is a
\displaystyle W
-invariant symmetric bilinear form on
\displaystyle\mathfrak{t}
and
\displaystyle E
is an extension of sheaf of abelian groups of the form

0\to\omega_{X}\to E\to\mathfrak{z}\tensor\mathcal{O}_{X}\to 0.

Remark 2.1.1
.

The parameter
\displaystyle E
plays a technically significant but conceptually minor role in the story. For reading of the main proof it is safe to ignore it on the first pass.

Let
\displaystyle\mathfrak{g}_{1},\ldots,\mathfrak{g}_{r}
be the simple factors of
\displaystyle\mathfrak{g}
, then
\displaystyle\kappa
can always be written uniquely as
\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{r}[c_{i}]\cdot\textnormal{Kil}_{i}+\mu_{\mathfrak{z}}
, where
\displaystyle\mu_{\mathfrak{z}}\in\textnormal{Sym}^{2}(\mathfrak{z}^{*})
,
\displaystyle\textnormal{Kil}_{i}
is the Killing form on
\displaystyle\mathfrak{g}_{i}
and we set
\displaystyle[c_{i}]:=\frac{c_{i}-h_{i}^{\vee}}{2h_{i}^{\vee}}
for
\displaystyle c_{i}\in\mathbb{C}
,
\displaystyle h_{i}^{\vee}
being the dual Coxeter number of
\displaystyle\mathfrak{g}_{i}
.
We write
\displaystyle\kappa_{\textnormal{crit},G}:=-\frac{1}{2}\textnormal{Kil}_{\mathfrak{g}}
and refer to
\displaystyle[\kappa_{\textnormal{crit},G},0]
as the critical level; note that it corresponds to
\displaystyle c_{i}=0
for each
\displaystyle i
. We refer to levels where each
\displaystyle c_{i}\in\mathbb{Q}^{<0}
(resp.
\displaystyle\mathbb{Q}^{>0},\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}
) as
negative
(resp.
positive
,
irrational
,
integral
).

Convention 2.1.2

(Critical Shift)
.

The superscript
\displaystyle\kappa
(without the square bracket) will always denote the
critically shifted
level
\displaystyle[\kappa+\kappa_{\textnormal{crit},G},0]
. For a bilinear form
\displaystyle\kappa
, we let
\displaystyle-\kappa
denote the bilinear form reflected along
\displaystyle\kappa_{\textnormal{crit},G}
. In this article,
\displaystyle\kappa
will always be a
positive
level, and
\displaystyle-\kappa
always a negative level.

Langlands Duality

Langlands duality attaches to every
\displaystyle(G,T)
a dual group
\displaystyle(\check{G},\check{T})
whose root datum is
\displaystyle(\Lambda,\Delta,\check{\Lambda},\check{\Delta})
. We let
\displaystyle[\check{\kappa},\check{E}]
denote the
Langlands dual
parameter: on each simple factor it sends
\displaystyle c_{i}
to
\displaystyle-\frac{1}{d_{i}c_{i}}
where
\displaystyle d_{i}
is the lacing number of
\displaystyle\mathfrak{g}_{i}
, and
\displaystyle\check{E}
is the extension induced by
\displaystyle\mathfrak{z}\simeq\check{\mathfrak{z}}
.

2.2
Factorizable Kazhdan–Lusztig Category

At this point we will start to freely use the theory of factorizable renormalized ind-coherent sheaves developed in Section
11
. The reader is suggested to take on faith the following claim, which summarizes the main output of said theory, and refer to the appendix when necessary.

Claim 2.2.1
.

For a class of sufficiently nice prestacks
\displaystyle\mathcal{Y}
, there exists a compactly generated DG category
\displaystyle\textnormal{IndCoh}_{*,\textnormal{ren}}(\mathcal{Y})
equipped with a (not necessarily left complete)
\displaystyle t
-structure, such that the bounded below category coincides with that of
\displaystyle\textnormal{QCoh}(\mathcal{Y})
. We let
\displaystyle\textnormal{IndCoh}^{!,\textnormal{ren}}(\mathcal{Y})
denote its dual category.

Let
\displaystyle B_{\textnormal{dR}}
be the de Rham prestack associated with a laft prestack
\displaystyle B
(we shall mostly consider
\displaystyle B=\textnormal{Ran}
). Suppose
\displaystyle\mathcal{Y}\to B_{\textnormal{dR}}
is a prestack whose fiber at every
\displaystyle x:\textnormal{pt}\to B_{\textnormal{dR}}
is reasonably nice. Then there exists a
crystal of categories

\displaystyle\mathcal{I}nd\mathcal{C}oh_{*,\textnormal{ren}}(\mathcal{Y})
(and a dual version
\displaystyle\mathcal{I}nd\mathcal{C}oh^{!,\textnormal{ren}}(\mathcal{Y})
) over
\displaystyle B_{\textnormal{dR}}
, whose fiber at every
\displaystyle x
is given by the renormalized ind-coherent sheaf category
\displaystyle\textnormal{IndCoh}_{*,\textnormal{ren}}(Y_{x})
(resp.
\displaystyle\textnormal{IndCoh}^{!,\textnormal{ren}}(Y_{x})
).

To each quantum parameter
\displaystyle[\kappa,E]
attached to a reductive group
\displaystyle H
(in our use cases we only consider
\displaystyle H=G
and
\displaystyle H=T
) we can associate an (unital) factorization line bundle
\displaystyle\mathscr{L}_{[\kappa,E]}
on

[\widehat{\textnormal{Hecke}}_{H}]_{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{dR}}}:=[\mathcal{L}^{+}H]_{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{dR}}}\backslash([\mathcal{L}H]_{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{dR}}})_{[\mathcal{L}^{+}H]_{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{dR}}}}^{\wedge}/[\mathcal{L}^{+}H]_{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{dR}}}

which admits a multiplicative structure under convolution (c.f. Proposition
13.0.1
). By restricting, we can also consider
\displaystyle\mathscr{L}_{[\kappa,E]}
as a factorization line bundle for
\displaystyle[\widehat{\textnormal{Hecke}}_{H^{\prime}}]_{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{dR}}}
,
\displaystyle H^{\prime}\subseteq H
any affine subgroup.

We have the following key construction, whose details are deferred to Section
3
.

Let
\displaystyle H
be a finite type affine algebraic group, and let
\displaystyle\mathscr{L}
be a unital factorization line bundle on
\displaystyle[\widehat{\textnormal{Hecke}}_{H}]_{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{dR}}}
.
Let
\displaystyle\mathcal{R}ep(\mathcal{L}^{+}H)
denote
\displaystyle\mathcal{I}nd\mathcal{C}oh^{!,\textnormal{ren}}(\mathbb{B}\mathcal{L}^{+}H)
; this category admits a unital factorization category structure. The category
\displaystyle\mathcal{I}nd\mathcal{C}oh^{!,\textnormal{ren}}([\widehat{\textnormal{Hecke}}_{H}]_{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{dR}}})
acts on it in a way compatible with the factorization structure. We set

\mathcal{KL}(H)_{\mathscr{L}}:=\mathscr{L}\operatorname{-mod}(\mathcal{R}ep(\mathcal{L}^{+}H))

and refer to it as the factorizable Kazhdan–Lusztig category; it again possesses the structure of a unital factorization category.

Because the category
\displaystyle\mathcal{R}ep(\mathcal{L}^{+}H)
is canonically self-dual (Remark
3.2.2
), it also admits a left action by
\displaystyle\mathcal{I}nd\mathcal{C}oh_{*,\textnormal{ren}}([\widehat{\textnormal{Hecke}}_{H}]_{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{dR}}})
. Dualizing, we obtain a
right
action by
\displaystyle\mathcal{I}nd\mathcal{C}oh^{!,\textnormal{ren}}(\mathbb{B}\mathcal{L}^{+}H)
on it. We define
7
7

7

The meaning of the negative sign in
\displaystyle\mathcal{KL}_{*}(H)_{\mathscr{L}^{-1}}
will be clear in Remark
3.3.12
.

\mathcal{KL}(H)_{\mathscr{L}^{-1},\textnormal{co}}:=\mathscr{L}\operatorname{-mod}^{r}(\mathcal{Rep}(\mathcal{L}^{+}H));

One can also think of
\displaystyle\mathcal{KL}(H)_{\mathscr{L}^{-1},\textnormal{co}}
as the dual factorization category of
\displaystyle\mathcal{KL}(H)_{\mathscr{L}}
(Remark
3.3.13
).

A salient feature of this category is the existence of an equivalence of unital factorization categories (Theorem
3.4.1
)

\mathcal{KL}(H)_{\mathscr{L}}\simeq\mathcal{KL}(H)_{\mathscr{L}\tensor\mathscr{L}^{\textnormal{Tate}},\textnormal{co}}

where
\displaystyle\mathscr{L}^{\textnormal{Tate}}
is the Tate twist associated with
\displaystyle H
(c.f. Examples
3.3.9
). Over each closed point
\displaystyle x
,
\displaystyle\mathscr{L}^{\textnormal{Tate}}
is the unique line bundle whose pullback to
\displaystyle[\mathcal{L}H]_{\mathcal{L}^{+}H}^{\wedge}
is the restriction of the determinant line bundle on
\displaystyle\mathcal{L}H
; over the entire curve, however, it involves an additional
\displaystyle E
-term.

Example 2.2.2
.

Let
\displaystyle\check{Z}_{G}^{\circ}
be the dual torus to

(the neutral component of the center of

\displaystyle\textstyle{0}
\displaystyle\textstyle{0\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{\omega_{X}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}

As explained in Remark

Definition 2.2.3
.

By restriction,
\displaystyle\mathscr{L}_{[\kappa+\kappa_{\textnormal{crit},G},0]}
can be also see as a line bundle over
\displaystyle H\backslash\mathcal{L}G_{\mathcal{L}^{+}G}^{\wedge}/H
for any compact open
\displaystyle H\subseteq\mathcal{L}^{+}G
. We define

\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{H}:=\mathscr{L}_{[\kappa+\kappa_{\textnormal{crit},G},0]}\operatorname{-mod}(\Rep(H));

here
\displaystyle\Rep(H):=\textnormal{IndCoh}^{!,\textnormal{ren}}(H)
is acted on by
\displaystyle\textnormal{IndCoh}^{!,\textnormal{ren}}(H\backslash\mathcal{L}G_{\mathcal{L}^{+}G}^{\wedge}/H)

This is likewise the renormalized derived category of
\displaystyle(\hat{\mathfrak{g}},H)
Harish-Chandra modules. We shall be mainly interested in
\displaystyle\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{I}
, known as the affine BGG category
\displaystyle\mathcal{O}
.

Let
\displaystyle\mathscr{L}:=\mathscr{L}_{[\kappa+\kappa_{\textnormal{crit},G},0]}
.
Fix a
\displaystyle\mathbb{C}
-point
\displaystyle x
on the curve
\displaystyle X
. As explained in Section

, this category extends to a
\displaystyle\mathcal{KL}(G)_{\mathscr{L}}

\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathcal{L}\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\mathscr{L}}^{\mathcal{L}^{+}G\times_{G_{x}}B_{x}}

Letting

also denote the restriction along

, then we have a (c.f. Construction

) factorizable functor

\textnormal{res}:\widetilde{\mathcal{L}\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\mathscr{L}}^{\mathcal{L}^{+}G\times_{G_{x}}B_{x}}\to\mathcal{KL}(B)_{\mathscr{L}}

defined by
\displaystyle!
-pullback of ind-coherent sheaves. On the other hand,
\displaystyle*

-IndCoh category) gives a (lax-unital) factorization functor

C^{\frac{\infty}{2}}:\mathcal{KL}(B)_{\mathscr{L}}\simeq\mathcal{KL}(B)_{\mathscr{L}\tensor\mathscr{L}^{\textnormal{Tate}}_{B},\textnormal{co}}\to\mathcal{KL}(T)_{\mathscr{L}_{[\kappa,E_{\textnormal{anom}}]},\textnormal{co}}\simeq\mathcal{KL}(T)_{\mathscr{L}_{[\kappa,E_{\textnormal{anom}}]}};

The meaning of the superscript will become evident in the next subsection.

2.3
Affine Lie algebra Representations

In this section, we collect some facts about
\displaystyle\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{I}

and
[

Convention 2.3.1
.

In this subsection only,
\displaystyle\kappa
will denote any non-critical level unless specified otherwise.

Definition 2.3.2
.

For each
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}\in\check{\Lambda}^{+}
, we have the Weyl modules

\mathbb{V}_{\kappa}^{\check{\lambda}}:=\textnormal{Ind}_{\mathcal{L}^{+}\mathfrak{g}\oplus\mathbb{C}}^{\hat{\mathfrak{g}}}V^{\check{\lambda}}\in\textnormal{KL}(G)_{\kappa}^{\heartsuit},

where
\displaystyle V^{\check{\lambda}}
is the standard finite-dimensional irreducible representation of
\displaystyle G
.
We shall refer to
\displaystyle\mathbb{V}^{0}_{\kappa}
as the
vacuum
representation at level
\displaystyle\kappa
.

Definition 2.3.3
.

Similarly, for each
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}\in\check{\Lambda}
, we have the affine Verma module

\mathbb{M}_{\kappa}^{\check{\lambda}}:=\textnormal{Ind}_{\textnormal{Lie}(I)}^{\hat{\mathfrak{g}}}k^{\check{\lambda}}\in\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{I,\heartsuit},

We let
\displaystyle\mathbb{M}_{\kappa}^{{\check{\lambda}},\vee}
denote the dual affine Verma modules, which are their right orthogonals, i.e. the unique object in
\displaystyle\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{I}
satisfying

\textnormal{Hom}_{\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{I}}(\mathbb{M}_{\kappa}^{\check{\lambda}},\mathbb{M}_{\kappa}^{{\check{\lambda}}^{\prime},\vee})=\begin{cases}k&\textnormal{if }{\check{\lambda}}={\check{\lambda}}^{\prime},\\
0&\textnormal{otherwise.}\end{cases}

Definition 2.3.4

(Averaging)
.

For every
\displaystyle K_{1}\subseteq K_{2}
, we let
\displaystyle\textnormal{Av}_{*}^{K_{2}/K_{1}}
denote the right adjoint to the forgetful functor
\displaystyle\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{K_{2}}\to\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{K_{1}}
.

Definition 2.3.5

(Categorical Duality)
.

Our general study of ind-coherent sheaves, in particular Theorem
3.4.1
, recovers the classically known fact that for every compact open
\displaystyle H
there exists a duality pairing of categories

\langle-,-\rangle_{\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{H}}:\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{H}\tensor\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{-\kappa}^{H}\to\textnormal{Vect}

(c.f.
[
Gai21
, Section 1.3]
).

We let
\displaystyle\mathbb{D}_{\textnormal{KM}}
denote the resulting functor on compact objects
8
8

8

This ought not to cause confusion: the duality for different
\displaystyle H
are compatible under forgetful functors.
. This functor has the following properties:

•

For any
\displaystyle\kappa
and
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}
we have
\displaystyle\mathbb{D}_{\textnormal{KM}}(\mathbb{M}_{\kappa}^{{\check{\lambda}}})\simeq\mathbb{M}_{-\kappa}^{-{\check{\lambda}}-2\check{\rho}}[\dim(\mathfrak{n})]
;

•

For any
\displaystyle\kappa
we have
\displaystyle\mathbb{D}_{\textnormal{KM}}(\mathbb{V}_{\kappa}^{0})\simeq\mathbb{V}_{-\kappa}^{0}
.

Highest Weight Structure

The collection of objects
\displaystyle\mathbb{M}_{\kappa}^{{\check{\lambda}}}
and
\displaystyle\mathbb{M}_{\kappa}^{{\check{\lambda}},\vee}
form a
highest weight structure
for
\displaystyle\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{I}
. However, it turns out that they do not correspond to the
quantum
(dual) Verma modules under our equivalence. Instead, we will have to use the following objects:

Definition 2.3.6
.

At
\displaystyle\kappa
positive (or irrational), we will refer to

\Delta_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}^{{\check{\lambda}}}:=\mathbb{D}_{\textnormal{KM}}(\mathbb{W}_{-\kappa}^{1,-{\check{\lambda}}-2\check{\rho}}[\dim(\mathfrak{n})])

as the
standard object
of highest weight
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}
, and

\nabla_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}^{{\check{\lambda}}}:=\mathbb{W}_{\kappa}^{w_{0},{\check{\lambda}}}

as the
costandard object
of highest weight
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}
. Here
\displaystyle 1
and
\displaystyle w_{0}
are respectively the shortest and longest element in the finite Weyl group, and
\displaystyle\mathbb{W}_{\kappa}^{w,{\check{\lambda}}}
is the
Wakimoto
module of level
\displaystyle\kappa
, type
\displaystyle w
and highest weight
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}
.

To define Wakimoto modules and check that the definition is valid (i.e. that
\displaystyle\mathbb{W}_{-\kappa}^{1,-{\check{\lambda}}-2\check{\rho}}
is compact), we need a bit more representation theory.

Sheaves on Affine Flag Variety

Let
\displaystyle I^{\circ}
denote the unipotent radical of
\displaystyle I
, i.e. the preimage of
\displaystyle N
under
\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{+}G\xrightarrow{t=0}G
. Let
\displaystyle\textnormal{Fl}_{G}:=\mathcal{L}G/I
denote the affine flag variety, and
\displaystyle\widetilde{\textnormal{Fl}_{G}}:=\mathcal{L}G/I^{\circ}
denote the enhanced affine flag variety.

As in
[
FG06
, Section 20.4]
, for each
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}\in\check{\Lambda}
the pair
\displaystyle(-\kappa,{\check{\lambda}})
determines a twisting on
\displaystyle\textnormal{Fl}_{G}
, and we let
\displaystyle\textnormal{DMod}_{(-\kappa,{\check{\lambda}})}(\textnormal{Fl}_{G})
denote the resulting category of twisted D-modules. When
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}=0
, we will simply use the subscript
\displaystyle-\kappa
.
The category
\displaystyle\textnormal{DMod}_{-\kappa}(\textnormal{Fl}_{G})^{I}
admits a monoidal structure known as
convolution
, which we will denote by
\displaystyle\star
. It acts on
\displaystyle\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{-\kappa}^{I}
via this convolution structure as well.

Metaplectic Duality

Take
\displaystyle\kappa
non-critical, then we can consider
\displaystyle\kappa
as a symmetric bilinear form on
\displaystyle\Lambda
. Assume
\displaystyle\kappa
is
rational
, which means its values are torsion as elements in
\displaystyle\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{Z}
. Let
\displaystyle\Lambda^{\sharp}
be its kernel, and
\displaystyle\check{\Lambda}^{\sharp}
the dual lattice to
\displaystyle\Lambda^{\sharp}
.
To each
\displaystyle\alpha\in\Delta
, we attach an element
\displaystyle\textnormal{ord}(q(\alpha))\cdot\alpha
where
\displaystyle q(\alpha):=\frac{\kappa(\alpha,\alpha)}{2}\in\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{Z}
; these form a set
\displaystyle\Delta^{\sharp}
. Similarly, we form
\displaystyle\check{\Delta}^{\sharp}\subseteq\check{\Delta}\tensor_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{Q}
by attaching to each
\displaystyle\check{\alpha}
the element
\displaystyle\frac{1}{\textnormal{ord}(q(\alpha))}\cdot\check{\alpha}
.

\displaystyle(\check{\Lambda}^{\sharp},\check{\Delta}^{\sharp},\Lambda^{\sharp},\Delta^{\sharp})
form another root datum, corresponding to a pair
\displaystyle(G^{\sharp},T^{\sharp})
.

Definition 2.3.7
.

We let
\displaystyle(H,T_{H})
be the Langlands dual of
\displaystyle(G^{\sharp},T^{\sharp})
and call it the
metaplectic dual
of
\displaystyle(G,T)
. (For instance, at integral levels we have
\displaystyle(H,T_{H})\simeq(\check{G},\check{T})
.) For convenience’s sake, we extend this definition to all levels by declaring the metaplectic datum to be trivial when
\displaystyle\kappa
is irrational.

We let
\displaystyle W^{\textnormal{aff},\textnormal{ext},\sharp}:=W^{\textnormal{fin}}\ltimes{\Lambda^{\sharp}}\subseteq W^{\textnormal{aff},\textnormal{ext}}
denote the extended affine Weyl group corresponding to
\displaystyle{\Lambda^{\sharp}}
.

Definition 2.3.8
.

For
\displaystyle\tilde{w}\in W^{\textnormal{aff},\textnormal{ext},\sharp}
, we let
\displaystyle j_{\tilde{w},*},j_{\tilde{w},!}\in\textnormal{DMod}_{-\kappa}(\textnormal{Fl}_{G})^{I}
denote the
\displaystyle!
and
\displaystyle*
-extensions of the constant sheaf supported on the orbit
\displaystyle I\tilde{w}I/I
of
\displaystyle\textnormal{Fl}_{G}
; we normalize them such that
\displaystyle!
-fibers at
\displaystyle\tilde{w}
is placed in degree
\displaystyle\ell(w)
, and refer to them as (co)standard sheaves on the affine flag variety.

These (co)standard sheaves satisfy the following properties:

•

For
\displaystyle\tilde{w}_{1},\tilde{w}_{2}
such that
\displaystyle\ell(\tilde{w}_{1})+\ell(\tilde{w}_{2})=\ell(\tilde{w}_{1}\tilde{w_{2}})
, we have

j_{\tilde{w}_{1},*}\star j_{\tilde{w}_{2},*}\simeq j_{\tilde{w}_{1}\tilde{w}_{2},*}\hskip 10.00002ptj_{\tilde{w}_{1},!}\star j_{\tilde{w}_{2},!}\simeq j_{\tilde{w}_{1}\tilde{w}_{2},!}

•

\displaystyle j_{\tilde{w},*}\star j_{\tilde{w}^{-1},!}\simeq\delta_{1}\simeq j_{\tilde{w}^{-1},!}\star j_{\tilde{w},*}
;

We will write
\displaystyle j_{\mu,!}
(resp.
\displaystyle j_{\mu,*}
) for
\displaystyle\mu\in{\Lambda^{\sharp}}
by considering it as a subgroup of
\displaystyle W^{\textnormal{aff},\textnormal{ext},\sharp}
.

Next we introduce
Wakimoto
sheaves on the affine flag variety, which is a collection of objects
\displaystyle\{J_{\lambda}\}_{\lambda\in{\Lambda^{\sharp}}}\in\textnormal{DMod}_{-\kappa}(\textnormal{Fl}_{G})^{I}
such that
9
9

9

We follow the convention of
[
Gai21
]
which is opposite from that of
[
AB09
]
.

•

For
\displaystyle\mu\in({\Lambda^{\sharp}})^{-}
we have
\displaystyle J_{\mu}\simeq j_{\mu,*}
;

•

For
\displaystyle\mu\in({\Lambda^{\sharp}})^{+}
we have
\displaystyle J_{\mu}\simeq j_{\mu,!}
;

•

For any
\displaystyle\mu_{1},\mu_{2}\in{\Lambda^{\sharp}}
we have
\displaystyle J_{\mu_{1}}\star J_{\mu_{2}}\simeq J_{\mu_{1}+\mu_{2}}
.

For convenience’s sake we will also extend the definition to all of
\displaystyle W^{\textnormal{aff},\textnormal{ext},\sharp}
by declaring
\displaystyle J_{\tilde{w}}:=J_{\mu}\star j_{w_{f}}
where
\displaystyle\tilde{w}=\mu w_{f},\mu\in{\Lambda^{\sharp}},w_{f}\in W_{\textnormal{fin}}
. For more details regarding these objects in at rational levels, see
[
Yan21
, Section 5]
.

Warning 2.3.9
.

We warn that we are
not
keeping track of the cotangent fiber as defined in

Kashiwara-Tanisaki Localization

We have an
IndCoh
-global section functor

\Gamma_{-\kappa}(\textnormal{Fl}_{G},-)^{I^{\circ}}:\textnormal{DMod}_{(-\kappa,{\check{\lambda}})}(\textnormal{Fl}_{G})^{I^{\circ}}\to\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{-\kappa}^{I^{\circ}}

as in
[
KT96
]

10
10

10

Because our Kac-Moody category is renormalized, some care is needed in comparing it with the classical notion; we refer readers to
[
Ras20
, Appendix A]
for more discussion.
. This functor also respects the remaining strong
\displaystyle T
-action, and we have an induced functor on the strong
\displaystyle T
-invariants:

\Gamma_{-\kappa}(\textnormal{Fl}_{G},-)^{I}:\textnormal{DMod}_{(-\kappa,{\check{\lambda}})}(\textnormal{Fl}_{G})^{I}\to\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{-\kappa}^{I}

Definition 2.3.10
.

An element
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}\in\check{\Lambda}
is called
\displaystyle\kappa
-admissible if:

•

\displaystyle\langle\alpha,{\check{\lambda}}+\check{\rho}\rangle\not\in\mathbb{Z}^{>0}
every positive coroot
\displaystyle\alpha
; and

•

\displaystyle\langle\alpha,{\check{\lambda}}+\check{\rho}\rangle+n\cdot\frac{-\kappa(\alpha,\alpha)}{2}\not\in\mathbb{Z}^{>0}
every positive coroot
\displaystyle\alpha
and every
\displaystyle n\in\mathbb{Z}^{>0}
.

Theorem 2.3.11

(
[
KT96
]
)
.

If
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}
is
\displaystyle\kappa
-admissible, then the functor
\displaystyle\Gamma_{-\kappa}(\textnormal{Fl}_{G},-)^{I^{\circ}}
and
\displaystyle\Gamma_{-\kappa}(\textnormal{Fl}_{G},-)^{I}
are
\displaystyle t
-exact, send each standard sheaf
\displaystyle j_{\tilde{w},!}
to
\displaystyle\mathbb{M}_{-\kappa}^{\tilde{w}\cdot{\check{\lambda}}}
and each costandard sheaf
\displaystyle j_{\tilde{w},*}
to
\displaystyle\mathbb{M}_{-\kappa}^{\tilde{w}\cdot{\check{\lambda}},\vee}
.

Remark 2.3.12
.

Under the more stringent condition of
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}
being
regular
\displaystyle\kappa
-admissible
(which means replacing
\displaystyle\not\in\mathbb{Z}^{>0}
with
\displaystyle\not\in\mathbb{Z}^{\geq 0}
in Definition
2.3.10
), it is also known that
\displaystyle\Gamma_{-\kappa}(\textnormal{Fl}_{G},-)^{I^{\circ}}
is a fully faithful embedding of a direct summand of
\displaystyle\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{-\kappa}^{I^{\circ}}
(c.f.
[
FG09a
, Theorem 5.5]
). We do not invoke this version.

Semi-infinite Cohomology

We refer readers to
