Main Computations

8.1
Proof of Theorem
2.6.3

We proceed in steps.

Preparation

For each
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}\in\check{\Lambda}
let
\displaystyle\iota_{{\check{\lambda}}\cdot x_{0}}
denote the inclusion of the point
\displaystyle({\check{\lambda}}\cdot x_{0})
into the marked configuration space. The costandard object
\displaystyle\nabla_{\textnormal{Conf},\kappa}^{\check{\mu}}
is uniquely characterized by its right orthogonal property with the standard objects
\displaystyle\Delta_{\textnormal{Conf},\kappa}^{{\check{\lambda}}}
; since the latter corepresent
\displaystyle!
-fiber at
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}\cdot x_{0}
, we see that
\displaystyle\nabla_{\textnormal{Conf},\kappa}^{\check{\mu}}
is the unique factorization module
\displaystyle M
that satisfies

\iota_{{\check{\lambda}}\cdot x_{0}}^{!}(M)\simeq\begin{cases}\mathbb{C}&{\check{\lambda}}=\check{\mu}\\
0&\textnormal{else}\end{cases};

However, by construction,
\displaystyle\textbf{J}_{\kappa}(\nabla_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}^{{\check{\lambda}}})
exactly satisfies this property.

Now recall that the standard objects form a set of compact generators of the source category (Lemma
2.3.16
). On the other hand,
\displaystyle\Delta_{\textnormal{Conf},\kappa}^{{\check{\lambda}}}
also compactly generates. It therefore suffices to show that
\displaystyle\textbf{J}^{\textnormal{KM}}_{\kappa}
sends standard to standard, and is fully faithful on these standard objects.
The latter fact is, in fact, obvious, as we have

\Hom_{\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{I}}(\Delta_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}^{{\check{\lambda}}},\Delta_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}^{\check{\mu}})\simeq C^{\frac{\infty}{2}}(\mathcal{L}\mathfrak{n},\mathcal{L}^{+}\mathfrak{n},\Delta_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}^{\check{\mu}})^{{\check{\lambda}}}

\simeq\Hom_{\Omega^{\textnormal{Lus}}_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}\textnormal{-FactMod}_{\textnormal{nu}}(\textnormal{DMod}_{[\check{\kappa},0]_{\leftarrow\omega^{\check{\rho}}}}(\textnormal{Conf}_{\infty\cdot x_{0}}))}(\Delta_{\textnormal{Conf},\kappa}^{{\check{\lambda}}},\Delta_{\textnormal{Conf},\kappa}^{\check{\mu}}).

Because of the right orthogonality characterization of the standard objects, it suffices to prove that

\iota_{\mu\cdot x_{0}}^{*}(\textbf{J}_{\kappa}(\Delta_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}^{{\check{\lambda}}}))\simeq\begin{cases}\mathbb{C}&{\check{\lambda}}=\check{\mu}\\
0&\textnormal{else}\end{cases}

Adding One Point

To do this we invoke the local-global compatibility by switching to the complete curve
\displaystyle\overline{X}\simeq\mathbb{P}^{1}
. We let
\displaystyle x_{\infty}\in\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{C})
denote the added point, and set
\displaystyle\overrightarrow{x}:=(x_{0},x_{\infty})
. The definition of Jacquet functor proceeds in the exact same way to give

\textbf{J}_{\kappa,\overrightarrow{x}}:(\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{I})_{x_{0}}\tensor(\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{I})_{x_{\infty}}\to\Omega^{\textnormal{Lus}}_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}\textnormal{-FactMod}_{\textnormal{nu}}(\textnormal{DMod}_{[\check{\kappa},0]_{\leftarrow\omega^{\check{\rho}}}}(\textnormal{Conf}_{\infty\cdot\overrightarrow{x}}(\mathbb{P}^{1}))).

Let

\textnormal{AJ}:\textnormal{Conf}_{\infty\cdot\overrightarrow{x}}(\mathbb{P}^{1})\subseteq[\textnormal{Gr}^{\omega^{\check{\rho}}}_{\check{T}}(\mathbb{P}^{1})]_{\textnormal{Ran}_{\overrightarrow{x},\textnormal{dR}}}\to\textnormal{Bun}_{\check{T}}(\mathbb{P}^{1})

denote the Abel-Jacobi map, given by
35
35

35

Note that

.

\sum_{i}{\check{\lambda}}_{i}\cdot x_{i}\mapsto\sum_{i}\mathcal{O}(-x_{i})\tensor{\check{\lambda}}_{i}\in\textnormal{Pic}(\mathbb{P}^{1})\tensor_{\mathbb{Z}}\check{\Lambda}\simeq\textnormal{Bun}_{\check{T}}(\mathbb{P}^{1}).

The gerbe

We let

For any

We remind readers that the latter, known as the

\langle\mathcal{F},(j_{U})_{\textnormal{co},*}\circ r_{*}(\omega_{\textnormal{pt}/N})\rangle_{\textnormal{DMod}(\textnormal{Bun}_{G}(\mathbb{P}^{1})^{\textnormal{level}_{B},\overrightarrow{x}})}

for

the inclusion of the trivial bundle. Thus we arrive at the expression

This fiber is provided by the (cohomologically shifted) chiral homology (over

\displaystyle(\Delta_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}^{{\check{\lambda}}},\nabla_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}^{2\check{\rho}-\check{\mu}})

supported at
\displaystyle 0
and
\displaystyle\infty

4.4.16
.
As is classically known, this is the coinvariant

C_{*}(\mathfrak{g}[t,t^{-1}],(\Delta_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}^{{\check{\lambda}}})_{0}\tensor(\nabla_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}^{2\check{\rho}-\check{\mu}})_{\infty}),

where
\displaystyle t
is the coordinate around
\displaystyle 0\in\mathbb{P}^{1}
(we use subscript to remind ourselves of the local coordinates). Thus we have reduced the computation of
\displaystyle*
-fiber to a representation-theoretic question.

Contragredient Duality

Using weight space of the Sugawara
\displaystyle L_{0}
operator one can define the
contragredient dual
of
\displaystyle M\in(\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{I})^{\heartsuit}
(c.f.
[
AG
]
), which we denote by
\displaystyle M^{*}
. The key property of this contragredient dual is that

C_{*}(\mathfrak{g}[t,t^{-1}],M_{0}\tensor(N^{*})_{\infty})\simeq\Hom_{\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{T}}(M,N)^{*}.

The contragredient duality exchanges Verma module
\displaystyle\mathbb{M}^{{\check{\lambda}}}
with the contragredient Verma module
\displaystyle\mathbb{M}^{-{\check{\lambda}},I^{-}}

for the opposite Iwahori
\displaystyle I^{-}
. Likewise, it exchanges
\displaystyle\mathbb{W}_{\kappa}^{w_{0},{\check{\lambda}}}
with
\displaystyle\mathbb{W}_{\kappa}^{1,-{\check{\lambda}},I^{-}}
. We thus have

\displaystyle\displaystyle(C_{*}(\mathfrak{g}[t,t^{-1}],(\Delta_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}^{{\check{\lambda}}})_{0}\tensor(\nabla_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}^{2\check{\rho}-\check{\mu}})_{\infty})[-\dim(\mathfrak{n})])^{*}

\displaystyle\displaystyle\simeq

\displaystyle\displaystyle\Hom_{\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{T}}((\Delta_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}^{{\check{\lambda}}})_{0},(\nabla_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}^{2\check{\rho}-\check{\mu}})^{*})_{0})[\dim(\mathfrak{n})]

\displaystyle\displaystyle\simeq

\displaystyle\displaystyle\Hom_{\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{T}}(\Delta_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}^{{\check{\lambda}}},(\mathbb{W}_{\kappa}^{w_{0},2\check{\rho}-\check{\mu}})^{*})[\dim(\mathfrak{n})]

\displaystyle\displaystyle\simeq

\displaystyle\displaystyle\Hom_{\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{T}}(\Delta_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}^{{\check{\lambda}}},\mathbb{W}_{\kappa}^{1,\check{\mu}-2\check{\rho},I^{-}})[\dim(\mathfrak{n})]

\displaystyle\displaystyle\simeq

\displaystyle\displaystyle\Hom_{\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{I}}(\Delta_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}^{{\check{\lambda}}},\textnormal{Av}_{*,I/T}(\mathbb{W}_{\kappa}^{1,\check{\mu}-2\check{\rho},I^{-}}))[\dim(\mathfrak{n})]

\displaystyle\displaystyle\simeq

\displaystyle\displaystyle\Hom_{\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{I}}(\Delta_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}^{{\check{\lambda}}},\mathbb{W}_{\kappa}^{w_{0},\check{\mu}})

\displaystyle\displaystyle\simeq

\displaystyle\displaystyle C^{\frac{\infty}{2}}(\mathcal{L}\mathfrak{n},\mathcal{L}^{+}\mathfrak{n},\mathbb{W}_{\kappa}^{w_{0},\check{\mu}})^{{\check{\lambda}}}\simeq\begin{cases}\mathbb{C}&\textnormal{if}~{\check{\lambda}}=\check{\mu}\\
0&\textnormal{else}\end{cases}

which finishes the proof.

8.2
Proof of Proposition
2.9.5

Our notations are as follows:

•

Let
\displaystyle\mathscr{G}_{[\check{\kappa},0]_{\leftarrow\omega^{\check{\rho}}}}
be the gerbe on
\displaystyle[\textnormal{Gr}_{\check{T}}(\mathbb{A}^{1})]_{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{dR}}}
coming from the “
\displaystyle\check{\rho}
-shifted” FLE, as well as its restriction to
Conf
(for the constructible case, use its Riemann-Hilbert counterpart);

•

Let
\displaystyle\textnormal{Conf}^{\check{\lambda}}
denote the component of
Conf
where the total degree is
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}
, and let

\Delta_{\check{\lambda}}:X\xrightarrow{x\mapsto{\check{\lambda}}x}\textnormal{Conf}^{\check{\lambda}}

the main diagonal embedding,
\displaystyle j_{\check{\lambda}}
the complement open embedding;

•

Let
\displaystyle\textnormal{Conf}^{\circ}
the open part of
Conf
, consisting of tuples whose coefficients are all negative simple roots.

Remark 8.2.1
.

The
\displaystyle\check{\rho}
-shift has the following effect. Suppose
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}=\sum_{i}(-n_{i})\cdot\check{\alpha}_{i}
is a negative combination of simple roots, then the restriction of
\displaystyle\mathscr{G}_{[\check{\kappa},0]_{\leftarrow\omega^{\check{\rho}}}}
to
\displaystyle\textnormal{Conf}^{\check{\lambda}}
is given by (see
[
Gai21a
, 1.3.5]
)

\left(\bigotimes_{i}\mathcal{O}(-\Delta_{i}^{\prime})^{\check{\kappa}(\alpha_{i},\alpha_{i})/2}\right)\bigotimes\left(\bigotimes_{i\neq j}\mathcal{O}(-\Delta_{i,j})^{\check{\kappa}(\check{\alpha}_{i},\check{\alpha}_{j})}\right);

here
\displaystyle\Delta_{i}^{\prime}
is the diagonal divisor in the symmetric power of the curve
\displaystyle X^{(n_{i})}
corresponding to
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}
, the second product runs over all unordered pairs
\displaystyle i\neq j
, and
\displaystyle\Delta_{i,j}
is the incidence divisor in
\displaystyle X^{(n_{i})}\times X^{(n_{j})}
. Directly inspecting the formula, one sees that the gerbe is canonically trivial on the open part
\displaystyle\textnormal{Conf}^{\circ}
.

Under the assumption from Condition
1.1.3
,
[
Gai21a
]
defines a factorization
perverse sheaf

\displaystyle\Omega_{q}^{\textnormal{Lus}}
via a combinatorial procedure, which we recall now:

Definition 8.2.2
.

The factorizable algebra
\displaystyle\Omega_{q,\textnormal{alg}}^{\textnormal{Lus}}
(resp.
\displaystyle\Omega_{q,\textnormal{top}}^{\textnormal{Lus}}
) is the regular holonomic D-module (resp. perverse sheaf) defined via the following inductive procedure:

•

using the canonical trivialization of the gerbe on
\displaystyle\textnormal{Conf}^{\circ}
, we have the
sign local system
on
\displaystyle\textnormal{Conf}^{\circ}
;

•

by
stipulating
our sheaf is a factorization algebra, we may assume that the sheaf has been defined away from the image of
\displaystyle\Delta_{\check{\lambda}}
;

•

on
\displaystyle\textnormal{Conf}^{\check{\lambda}}
, if
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}
can be written as
\displaystyle w(\check{\rho})-\check{\rho}
for
\displaystyle\ell(w)=2
, we take
\displaystyle!*
-extension along
\displaystyle j_{\check{\lambda}}
(these encode the
quantum Serre relations
);

•

Otherwise, we take
\displaystyle H^{0}
of the
\displaystyle!
-extension along
\displaystyle j_{\check{\lambda}}
.

Convention 8.2.3
.

For arguments that apply to both algebraic and topological situation equally, we will simply write this factorization algebra as
\displaystyle\Omega_{q}^{\textnormal{Lus}}
.

As our next criterion demonstrates, this object enjoys strong rigidity property:

Proposition 8.2.4
.

\displaystyle\Omega_{q}^{\textnormal{Lus}}
is the
unique
non-unital Ran-constructible factorization algebra within

\textnormal{DMod}_{\mathscr{G}_{[\check{\kappa},0]_{\leftarrow\omega^{\check{\rho}}}}}([\textnormal{Gr}_{\check{T}}]_{\textnormal{Ran}})\hskip 5.0pt\textnormal{or}\hskip 5.0pt\textnormal{Shv}^{!}_{\textnormal{RH}(\mathscr{G}_{[\check{\kappa},0]_{\leftarrow\omega^{\check{\rho}}}})}([\textnormal{Gr}_{\check{T}}]_{\textnormal{Ran}})

satisfying the following cohomological estimates: for every
\displaystyle x\in X(\mathbb{C})
and every
\displaystyle\lambda\in\check{\Lambda}
,

1.

if
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}\notin\check{\Lambda}^{<0}
, then the
\displaystyle!
-fiber at
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}\cdot x
is zero;

2.

the
\displaystyle!
-fiber at every
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}\cdot x
has no negative cohomology;

3.

if
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}
is a simple negative root, then either the
\displaystyle*
-fiber at
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}\cdot x
is
\displaystyle\mathbb{C}[1]
, or the
\displaystyle!
-fiber at
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}\cdot x
is
\displaystyle\mathbb{C}[-1]
;

4.

if
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}
equals
\displaystyle w(\check{\rho})-\check{\rho}
for some
\displaystyle\ell(w)=2,w\in W_{\textnormal{fin}}
, then the
\displaystyle!
-fiber at
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}\cdot x
vanishes at
\displaystyle H^{0}
and
\displaystyle H^{1}
, and
\displaystyle*
-fiber at
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}\cdot x
vanishes at
\displaystyle H^{0}
and
\displaystyle H^{-1}
;

5.

otherwise, the
\displaystyle!
-fiber at
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}\cdot x
vanishes at
\displaystyle H^{0}
, and
\displaystyle*
-fiber at
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}\cdot x
vanishes at
\displaystyle H^{0}
,
\displaystyle H^{-1}
and
\displaystyle H^{-2}
.

Proof.

We first verify that
\displaystyle\Omega_{q}^{\textnormal{Lus}}
satisfies the conditions listed above. Condition (1) and (2) are evident; condition (3) is
[
Gai21a
, 3.5.9]
. For condition (4) and (5), (the Koszul dual of)
[
Gai21a
, 3.7.3, (a) and (b)]
gives the
\displaystyle*-
and
\displaystyle!
-estimate respectively, with the
\displaystyle!
-condition for (5) being evident.

Now suppose
\displaystyle\mathcal{F}
satisfies condition (1) to (5) above. Condition (1) guarantees that the sheaf is supported on the configuration space. Since the sheaf is locally constant along the diagonal stratification and has factorization property, condition (3) guarantees that it is the sign local system on the open locus. The vanishing condition on
\displaystyle H^{0}
from (2), (4) and (5) guarantee that
\displaystyle\mathcal{F}
is actually a perverse sheaf over the entire configuration space.

We will now show that
\displaystyle\mathcal{F}
is uniquely determined on each
\displaystyle\textnormal{Conf}^{\check{\lambda}}
by running induction on the total degree of
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}
. The base case is
\displaystyle|{\check{\lambda}}|=1
, which we already argued above. So we assume
\displaystyle|{\check{\lambda}}|\geq 2
. By factorization and induction, we can assume
\displaystyle\mathcal{F}
is already uniquely determined away from the main diagonal. Thus the proposition would follow from the following claims:

•

if
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}=w(\check{\rho})-\check{\rho}
for
\displaystyle\ell(w)=2
, then
\displaystyle\mathcal{F}\simeq H^{0}((j_{\check{\lambda}})_{!}(j_{\check{\lambda}})^{!}\mathcal{F})
;

•

otherwise,
\displaystyle\mathcal{F}\simeq(j_{\check{\lambda}})_{!*}(j_{\check{\lambda}})^{!}\mathcal{F}
.

For (b), note that we have an exact sequence

H^{0}((j_{\check{\lambda}})_{!}(j_{\check{\lambda}})^{!}(\mathcal{F}))\to\mathcal{F}\to H^{0}((\Delta_{{\check{\lambda}}})_{*}(\Delta_{{\check{\lambda}}})^{*}(\mathcal{F}))

and the last term vanishes by
\displaystyle*
-fiber condition in (4), which means the first arrow is surjective; at the same point, we also have the exact sequence

H^{0}((\Delta_{{\check{\lambda}}})_{!}(\Delta_{{\check{\lambda}}})^{!}(\mathcal{F}))\to\mathcal{F}\to H^{0}((j_{\check{\lambda}})_{*}(j_{\check{\lambda}})^{*}(\mathcal{F}))

and the first term vanishes by
\displaystyle!
-fiber condition in (4), so the second map is injective. So we have

H^{0}((j_{\check{\lambda}})_{!}(j_{\check{\lambda}})^{!}(\mathcal{F}))\surj\mathcal{F}\inj H^{0}((j_{\check{\lambda}})_{*}(j_{\check{\lambda}})^{*}(\mathcal{F}))

implying point (b). For (a), note that we have

H^{-1}((\Delta_{{\check{\lambda}}})_{*}(\Delta_{{\check{\lambda}}})^{*}(\mathcal{F}))\to H^{0}((j_{\check{\lambda}})_{!}(j_{\check{\lambda}})^{!}(\mathcal{F}))\to\mathcal{F}\to H^{0}((\Delta_{{\check{\lambda}}})_{*}(\Delta_{{\check{\lambda}}})^{*}(\mathcal{F}))

and the first and the last term vanish by the
\displaystyle*
-fiber estimate in (4).
∎

Our remaining job is to use this criterion to match the factorization algebras produced from both the Kac-Moody side and the quantum side.

8.2.5
Kac-Moody Side

Definition 8.2.6
.

Fixed a bilinear form
\displaystyle\kappa
. For each simple factor
\displaystyle\mathfrak{g}_{i}
of
\displaystyle\mathfrak{g}
, let
\displaystyle\kappa|_{\mathfrak{g}_{i}}=\frac{c-h_{i}^{\vee}}{2h_{i}^{\vee}}\textnormal{Kil}_{\mathfrak{g}_{i}}
; we say
\displaystyle\kappa
is
almost admissible
on
\displaystyle\mathfrak{g}_{i}
if either
\displaystyle c
is irrational, or
\displaystyle c=\frac{p}{q}
for coprime
\displaystyle p,q\in\mathbb{Z}^{>0}
, such that

p\geq\begin{cases}h_{i}^{\vee}-1&\textnormal{if}~(q,d_{i})=1\\
h_{i}-1&\textnormal{else}\end{cases}

here
\displaystyle d_{i}
is the lacing number of
\displaystyle\mathfrak{g}_{i}
, and
\displaystyle h_{i}
(resp.
\displaystyle h^{\vee}_{i}
) is the Coxeter (resp. dual Coxeter) number of
\displaystyle\mathfrak{g}_{i}
. We say
\displaystyle\kappa
is
almost admissible
if it is so on each simple factor of
\displaystyle\mathfrak{g}
.

Remark 8.2.7
.

We call this
almost admissible
because the lower bound on
\displaystyle p
is precisely 1 below that of the classical notion of admissibility as defined in
[
KW08
]
.

First observe that, even though
\displaystyle w\cdot(-2\check{\rho})
is not necessarily dominant, we still have

Lemma 8.2.8
.

When
\displaystyle\kappa
is almost admissible, the canonical map
\displaystyle\mathbb{M}_{-\kappa}^{w\cdot(-2\check{\rho})}\to\mathbb{W}_{-\kappa}^{1,w\cdot(-2\check{\rho})}
is an isomorphism for every
\displaystyle w\in W^{\textnormal{fin}}
.

Proof.

Choose sufficiently large
\displaystyle\mu\gg 0
such that
\displaystyle w\cdot(-2\check{\rho})+\kappa(\mu)\in\check{\Lambda}^{+}
. By
[
Gai21
, Section 3.4.3]
, we have

\mathbb{M}_{-\kappa}^{w\cdot(-2\check{\rho})+\kappa(\mu)}\simeq\mathbb{W}_{-\kappa}^{1,w\cdot(-2\check{\rho})+\kappa(\mu)};

by
[
Gai21
, Section 2.5.9]
, (and because
\displaystyle J_{\mu}\star\bullet
for
\displaystyle\mu\gg 0
is invertible,) the claim follows if we prove

j_{\mu,!}\star\mathbb{M}_{-\kappa}^{w\cdot(-2\check{\rho})}\simeq\mathbb{M}_{-\kappa}^{w\cdot(-2\check{\rho})+\kappa(\mu)}.

Note that
\displaystyle-2\check{\rho}
is
\displaystyle\kappa
-admissible weight by our assumption: the first condition of Definition
2.3.10
is trivial, and the second condition is guaranteed precisely when
\displaystyle\kappa
is almost admissible. Thus Theorem
2.3.11
can be invoked, and the claim above reduces to the following claim about
\displaystyle-\kappa
-twisted D-modules on the affine flag variety:

j_{\mu,!}\star j_{w,!}\simeq j_{\mu w,!};

this is guaranteed if we have
\displaystyle\ell(\mu)+\ell(w)=\ell(\mu w)
, which in turn follows from the following general length formula for elements in the extended affine Weyl group: for
\displaystyle\mu_{0}\in\Lambda
and
\displaystyle w_{0}\in W^{\textnormal{fin}}
, we have

\ell(\mu_{0}w_{0})=\sum_{\alpha\in\Delta^{+},w_{0}^{-1}(\alpha)\in\Delta^{+}}|\langle\mu_{0},\alpha\rangle|+\sum_{\alpha\in\Delta^{+},w_{0}^{-1}(\alpha)\in\Delta^{-}}|1+\langle\mu_{0},\alpha\rangle|.

∎

Corollary 8.2.9
.

When
\displaystyle\kappa
is positive and is almost admissible, there exists a BGG resolution

\left[0\to\Delta_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}^{w_{0}\cdot 0}\to\ldots\to\bigoplus_{w\in W^{\textnormal{fin}},\ell(w)=1}\Delta_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}^{w\cdot 0}\to\underline{\Delta_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}^{0}}\to 0\right]\simeq\mathbb{V}_{\kappa}^{0}

of the vacuum by standard objects at positive level. Here on LHS the underline marks cohomological degree
\displaystyle 0
(thus e.g. the object
\displaystyle\Delta_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}^{0}
is placed at cohomological degree 0).

Proof.

At level
\displaystyle-\kappa
, we have a standard BGG resolution of the vacuum by Verma modules

\left[0\to\mathbb{M}_{-\kappa}^{-2\check{\rho}}\to\bigoplus_{w\in W^{\textnormal{fin}},\ell(w)=1}\mathbb{M}_{-\kappa}^{w\cdot(-2\check{\rho})}\to\ldots\to\underline{\mathbb{M}_{-\kappa}^{w_{0}\cdot(-2\check{\rho})}}\to 0\right]\simeq\mathbb{V}_{-\kappa}^{0};

by Lemma
8.2.8
, this can be rewritten as

\left[0\to\mathbb{W}_{-\kappa}^{1,-2\check{\rho}}\to\bigoplus_{w\in W^{\textnormal{fin}},\ell(w)=1}\mathbb{W}_{-\kappa}^{1,w\cdot(-2\check{\rho})}\to\ldots\to\underline{\mathbb{W}_{-\kappa}^{1,w_{0}\cdot(-2\check{\rho})}}\to 0\right]\simeq\mathbb{V}_{-\kappa}^{0};

Given that
\displaystyle\mathbb{D}_{\textnormal{KM}}(\mathbb{V}_{-\kappa}^{0})\simeq\mathbb{V}_{\kappa}^{0}
, the original claim now follows from applying
\displaystyle\mathbb{D}_{\textnormal{KM}}
to the equation above (note that it flips the direction of arrows).
∎

The following estimates will be needed in light of Proposition
8.2.4
:

Proposition 8.2.10
.

If
\displaystyle\kappa
is positive and almost admissible,
\displaystyle\mathbb{V}_{\kappa}^{0}
is the vacuum module, then:

1.

We have

\Hom_{\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{I}}(\mathbb{V}_{\kappa}^{0},\nabla_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}^{{\check{\lambda}}})=\begin{cases}\mathbb{C}[-\ell(w_{f})]&{\check{\lambda}}=w_{f}(\check{\rho})-\check{\rho},w_{f}\in W^{\textnormal{fin}}\\
0&\textnormal{else}\end{cases}

2.

For every
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}\in\check{\Lambda}

\displaystyle C_{*}^{\frac{\infty}{2}}(\mathcal{L}\mathfrak{n},\mathcal{L}^{+}\mathfrak{n},\mathbb{V}_{\kappa}^{0})^{\check{\lambda}}
vanishes unless
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}\in\check{\Lambda}^{\leq 0}
, is concentrated in cohomological degree
\displaystyle\geq 0
, and is nonzero in degree
\displaystyle 0
only if
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}=0
;

3.

For
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}=w(\check{\rho})-\check{\rho}
,
\displaystyle w\in W^{\textnormal{fin}},\ell(w)=2
,
\displaystyle H^{1}(C_{*}^{\frac{\infty}{2}}(\mathcal{L}\mathfrak{n},\mathcal{L}^{+}\mathfrak{n},\mathbb{V}_{\kappa}^{0})^{\check{\lambda}})=0
.

Proof.

(1) follows directly from the previous corollary.

For (2), let
\displaystyle C:=C_{*}^{\frac{\infty}{2}}(\mathcal{L}\mathfrak{n},\mathcal{L}^{+}N,\mathbb{V}_{\kappa}^{0})
denote the semi-infinite complex for the vacuuum, and let
\displaystyle(\mathfrak{n}_{i})_{i\geq 0}
denote a sequence of compact-open subalgebras

\mathcal{L}^{+}\mathfrak{n}\simeq\mathfrak{n}_{0}\subset\mathfrak{n}_{1}\subset\ldots\subset\bigcup_{i\geq 0}\mathfrak{n}_{i}\simeq\mathcal{L}\mathfrak{n};

As in
[
Ras21
, Appendix A.8]
, one may impose a
\displaystyle\mathbb{Z}^{-}
-filtered PBW-type filtration

\ldots\subset F_{-1}C\subset F_{0}C\simeq C

on the semi-infinite chain complex, such that
\displaystyle\limit_{-i\to-\infty}F_{-i}C\simeq 0
and

\textnormal{gr}_{-i}C\simeq C^{*}(\mathcal{L}^{+}\mathfrak{n},\textnormal{Sym}^{i}(\mathcal{L}(\mathfrak{g}/\mathfrak{n})/\mathcal{L}^{+}(\mathfrak{g}/\mathfrak{n}))).

Note that for each
\displaystyle i
,
\displaystyle H^{\bullet}(\textnormal{gr}_{-i}C)^{{\check{\lambda}}}
is zero unless
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}\in\check{\Lambda}^{<0}
; we also have

H^{0}(\textnormal{gr}_{-i}C)\subseteq H^{0}(\mathfrak{n},\textnormal{Sym}^{i}(\mathfrak{g}/\mathfrak{n}))\subseteq\textnormal{Sym}(\mathfrak{g}/\mathfrak{n})^{\mathfrak{n}}\simeq\textnormal{Sym}(\mathfrak{h})

so we see that
\displaystyle H^{0}(\textnormal{gr}_{-i}C)^{{\check{\lambda}}}=0
unless
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}=0
. Now we have, within
\displaystyle\textnormal{KL}_{\kappa^{\prime}}(T)^{<0}
,

0\simeq\tau_{<0}~0\simeq\tau_{<0}\limit_{-i}F_{-i}C\simeq\limit_{-i}\tau_{<0}F_{-i}C;

as we have
\displaystyle\tau_{<0}~\textnormal{gr}_{-i}C\simeq 0
, from the usual exact triangle we see that
\displaystyle\tau_{<0}F_{-i-1}C\to\tau_{<0}F_{-i}C
is an isomorphism for each
\displaystyle i
, so that limit diagram is constant and each term is zero; in particular we have
\displaystyle\tau_{<0}C\simeq\tau_{<0}F_{0}C\simeq 0
. The other two claims of (2) now follows the same argument.

It remains to compute (3). We have

\Hom_{\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{I}}(\Delta_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}^{w_{f}\cdot 0},\mathbb{V}_{\kappa}^{0})\simeq\Hom_{\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{-\kappa}^{I}}(\mathbb{D}_{\textnormal{KM}}(\mathbb{V}_{\kappa}^{0}),\mathbb{D}_{\textnormal{KM}}(\Delta_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}^{w_{f}\cdot 0}))

\simeq\Hom_{\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{-\kappa}^{I}}(\mathbb{V}_{-\kappa}^{0},\mathbb{W}_{-\kappa}^{1,w_{f}\cdot(-2\check{\rho})}[\dim(\mathfrak{n})])\simeq\Hom_{\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{-\kappa}^{I}}(\mathbb{V}_{-\kappa}^{0},\mathbb{M}_{-\kappa}^{w_{f}\cdot(-2\check{\rho})})[\dim(\mathfrak{n})],

where in the last step we used Lemma
8.2.8
above.
Because
\displaystyle\kappa
is almost admissible, we can invoke Kashiwara-Tanisaki for the weight
\displaystyle(-2\check{\rho})
. Consider the closed embedding of the basic affine space

\iota_{\textnormal{Fin}}:G/B\to\mathcal{L}^{+}G/I\simeq\textnormal{Fl}_{\textnormal{G}};

the weight
\displaystyle(-2\check{\rho})
determines a twisting on
\displaystyle G/B
that is compatible with
\displaystyle(-\kappa,-2\check{\rho})
via pullback along
\displaystyle\iota_{\textnormal{Fin}}
, so we have a well-defined functor
\displaystyle\iota_{\textnormal{Fin},!}:\textnormal{DMod}_{(-2\check{\rho})}(G/B)\to\textnormal{DMod}_{(-\kappa,-2\check{\rho})}(\textnormal{Fl}_{G})
, and an induced functor

\iota_{\textnormal{Fin},!}^{N}:\textnormal{DMod}_{(-2\check{\rho})}(G/B)^{N}\to\textnormal{DMod}_{(-\kappa,-2\check{\rho})}(\textnormal{Fl}_{G})^{I^{\circ}}.

For each
\displaystyle w_{f}\in W^{\textnormal{fin}}
,
\displaystyle j_{\textnormal{Fin},w_{f},!}
(resp.
\displaystyle j_{\textnormal{Fin},w_{f},*}
) denote the
\displaystyle!
(resp.
\displaystyle*
) extension on
\displaystyle G/B
of the IC sheaf of the corresponding
\displaystyle N
-orbit; these correspond to finite Verma (resp. dual Verma) modules under the usual Beilinson-Bernstein localization. We note that the
\displaystyle w_{f}
-orbits in the affine flag variety are isomorphic to these finite orbits under
\displaystyle\iota_{\textnormal{Fin}}
. Further observe that by base change we have

\Gamma_{-\kappa}(\textnormal{Fl}_{G},\textnormal{IC}_{G/B})^{I^{\circ}}\simeq\mathbb{V}_{-\kappa}^{0};

here in writing
\displaystyle\textnormal{IC}_{G/B}
we note that
\displaystyle(-2\check{\rho})
is integral. We claim that this means

\Hom_{\textnormal{DMod}_{(-\kappa,-2\check{\rho})}(\textnormal{Fl}_{G})^{I^{\circ}}}(\textnormal{IC}_{G/B},j_{w_{f},!})\simeq\Hom_{\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{-\kappa}^{I^{\circ}}}(\mathbb{V}_{-\kappa}^{0},\mathbb{M}_{-\kappa}^{w_{f}\cdot(-2\check{\rho})});

indeed,
\displaystyle\textnormal{IC}_{G/B}
admits a
finite
resolution by standard objects, and
\displaystyle j_{w_{f},!}
a
finite
resolution by costandard objects (
[
AB09
, Lemma 15]
). Because everything commutes with finite colimits, the claim follows from the fact that standard and costandard objects are orthogonals in both
\displaystyle\textnormal{DMod}_{(-\kappa,-2\check{\rho})}(\textnormal{Fl}_{G})^{I_{0}}
and
\displaystyle\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{-\kappa}^{I_{0}}
. Next, note that

\Hom_{\textnormal{DMod}_{-2\check{\rho}}(G/B)^{N}}(\textnormal{IC}_{G/B},j_{\textnormal{Fin},w_{f},!})[\dim(\mathfrak{n})]\simeq\Hom_{\mathfrak{g}\operatorname{-mod}^{N}}(k,\mathbb{M}_{\textnormal{fin}}^{w_{f}\cdot(-2\check{\rho})})[\dim(\mathfrak{n})]

\simeq\Hom_{\mathfrak{g}\operatorname{-mod}^{N}}(\mathbb{M}_{\textnormal{fin}}^{w_{f}\cdot 0},k)\simeq\mathbb{C}[-\ell(w_{f})]

where we use the finite analogue of
\displaystyle\mathbb{D}_{\textnormal{KM}}
in the middle. Now the claim original claim follows from the fact that

\Hom_{\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{-\kappa}^{I}}(\mathbb{V}_{-\kappa}^{0},\mathbb{M}_{-\kappa}^{w_{f}\cdot(-2\check{\rho})}[\dim(\mathfrak{n})])\simeq H_{T}^{*}(\Hom_{\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{-\kappa}^{I^{\circ}}}(\mathbb{V}_{-\kappa}^{0},\mathbb{M}_{-\kappa}^{w_{f}\cdot(-2\check{\rho})}[\dim(\mathfrak{n})])).

∎

Lemma 8.2.11
.

If
\displaystyle\kappa
is positive and almost admissible, we have
\displaystyle\Omega^{\textnormal{Lus}}_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}\simeq\Omega_{q,\textnormal{alg}}^{\textnormal{Lus}}
.

Proof.

Proposition
2.6.2
allows us to invoke Proposition
8.2.4
. We already know that the
\displaystyle!
-fibers of
\displaystyle\Omega^{\textnormal{Lus}}_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}
are given by semi-infinite cohomology of the vacuum; to interpret the
\displaystyle*
-fibers, we invoke Theorem
2.6.3
. Recall from Section
2.5.4
that the costandard object
\displaystyle\nabla_{\textnormal{Conf},\kappa}^{{\check{\lambda}}}
corepresent the functor of taking
\displaystyle*
-fibers at
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}\cdot x
within the factorization module category. Let
\displaystyle\iota_{{\check{\lambda}}\cdot x}
denote the inclusion, then we have

\iota_{{\check{\lambda}}\cdot x}^{*}(\Omega^{\textnormal{Lus}}_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa})\simeq\Hom_{\Omega^{\textnormal{Lus}}_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}\textnormal{-FactMod}_{\textnormal{nu}}(\textnormal{DMod}_{[\check{\kappa},0]_{\leftarrow\omega^{\check{\rho}}}}(\textnormal{Conf}_{\infty\cdot x_{0}}))}(\Omega^{\textnormal{Lus}}_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa},\nabla_{\textnormal{Conf},\kappa}^{{\check{\lambda}}})

\simeq\Hom_{\hat{\mathfrak{g}}\operatorname{-mod}_{\kappa}^{I}}(\mathbb{V}_{\kappa}^{0},\nabla_{\textnormal{KM},\kappa}^{{\check{\lambda}}}).

Now we can invoke (1) of Proposition
8.2.10
to finish the argument.
∎

8.2.12
Quantum Side

Recall that in
[
Gai21a
]
the factorization algebra
\displaystyle\Omega_{q}^{\textnormal{Lus}}
was related to
\displaystyle U_{q}^{\textnormal{KD}}(N^{-})\in\textnormal{BiAlg}(\Rep_{q}(T))
(defined in Definition
2.8.1
) by appealing to a general construction in
[
BFS06
]
that uses hyperbolic restriction to produce a factorizable perverse sheaf from a (graded) Hopf algebra in the heart. We take the following definition instead:

Definition 8.2.13
.

We define a topological factorization algebra
\displaystyle\Omega_{\mathbb{E}_{2},q}^{\textnormal{Lus}}
in the topological factorization category
\displaystyle\textnormal{Shv}^{!}_{\textnormal{RH}(\mathscr{G}_{[\check{\kappa},0]_{\leftarrow\omega^{\check{\rho}}}})}([\textnormal{Gr}_{\check{T}}]_{\textnormal{Ran}})
to be the image of

\textnormal{AugIdeal}(\textnormal{coBar}(U_{q}^{\textnormal{KD}}(N^{-})))\in\mathbb{E}_{2}\textnormal{-Alg}_{\textnormal{nu}}(\Rep_{q}(T))

under the equivalence in Proposition
6.3.8
.

Lemma 8.2.14
.

If
\displaystyle q
is non-degenerate, avoids small torsion and almost admissible, we have
\displaystyle\Omega_{\mathbb{E}_{2},q}^{\textnormal{Lus}}\simeq\Omega_{q,\textnormal{top}}^{\textnormal{Lus}}
.

Proof.

From Proposition
7.3.2
, using the fact that

\Hom_{U_{q}^{\textnormal{KD}}(N^{-})\textnormal{-comod}(\Rep_{q}(T))}(k,k)\simeq\Hom_{U_{q}^{\textnormal{Lus}}(N)\textnormal{-mod}_{\textnormal{loc.nilp}}(\Rep_{q}(T))}(k,k)\simeq\Hom_{U_{q}^{\textnormal{Lus}}(N)\textnormal{-mod}(\Rep_{q}(T))}(k,k)

as in
[
Gai21
, Lemma 4.3.5]
(note that
\displaystyle k
is
by definition
compact in
\displaystyle U_{q}^{\textnormal{Lus}}(N)\textnormal{-mod}_{\textnormal{loc.nilp}}(\Rep_{q}(T))
), it suffices to check that if
\displaystyle q
satisfies the conditions listed at the beginning of Section
2.7
, then we have the following cohomological estimates:

1.

\displaystyle C^{*}(U_{q}^{\textnormal{Lus}}(N),k)^{{\check{\lambda}}}
is zero unless
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}\in\check{\Lambda}^{<0}
, is always concentrated in degree
\displaystyle\geq 0
, and only has nonzero
\displaystyle H^{0}
if
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}=0
;

2.

If
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}
is a simple negative root, then
\displaystyle C_{*}(U_{q^{-1}}^{\textnormal{KD}}(N^{-}),k)^{{\check{\lambda}}}\simeq\mathbb{C}[1]
;

3.

If
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}=w(\check{\rho})-\check{\rho}
for
\displaystyle\ell(w)=2
,
\displaystyle w\in W_{\textnormal{fin}}
, then
\displaystyle H^{1}(U_{q}^{\textnormal{Lus}}(N),k)^{{\check{\lambda}}}\simeq 0
and
\displaystyle H_{1}(U_{q^{-1}}^{\textnormal{KD}}(N^{-}),k)^{{\check{\lambda}}}\simeq 0
;

4.

For every other
\displaystyle{\check{\lambda}}
, we have
\displaystyle H_{2}(U_{q^{-1}}^{\textnormal{KD}}(N^{-}),k)^{{\check{\lambda}}}\simeq 0
.

Consider the resolution of
\displaystyle k
given by

\ldots\xrightarrow{\delta_{2}}U\tensor\ker(\delta_{0})\xrightarrow{\delta_{1}}U\xrightarrow{\delta_{0}}k\to 0

for either
\displaystyle U=U_{q}^{\textnormal{Lus}}(N)
or
\displaystyle U=U_{q^{-1}}^{\textnormal{KD}}(N^{-})
. Here each
\displaystyle\delta_{i}
is the multiplication map (so
\displaystyle\delta_{0}
is the augmentation ideal). (1) and (2) then obvious. Both
\displaystyle H^{1}
in (3) are spanned by generators of the algebra, so (3) follows from the fact that none of the generators (for either algebra) has the prescribed form. For (4), note that
\displaystyle H_{2}
is a quotient of
\displaystyle\ker(I\tensor I\xrightarrow{m}I)
where
\displaystyle I
is the augmentation ideal of
\displaystyle U_{q^{-1}}^{\textnormal{KD}}(N^{-})
, i.e. the span of relations. As noted in
[
Gai21a
, Remark 3.3.7]
, when the parameter
\displaystyle q
satisfies said conditions, this space is spanned by quantum Serre relations and thus has no other weight.
∎

9
Apppendix A: Lax Limits

In this section we develop some basic properties of lax limits parallel to those in
[
AMR21
]
, which does not immediately follow from
loc.cit.
because we need to work with the unstable non-presentable setting.

Recall from
[
AMR21
]
the definition of a
lax limit

\displaystyle\mathsf{Glue}(\Phi)
corresponding to a
lax functor

\displaystyle\Phi:I\dashrightarrow\textnormal{Cat}
. Intuitively, given a poset
\displaystyle(I,>)
, a lax functor
\displaystyle\Phi
encodes the data

i\in\mathcal{I}\mapsto\Phi(i)\in\textnormal{Cat}\hskip 10.00002pt(i>j)\leadsto\Phi_{ij}:\Phi(i)\to\Phi(j)\hskip 10.00002pt(i>j>k)\leadsto\eta_{ijk}:\Phi_{jk}\circ\Phi_{ij}\Rightarrow\Phi_{ik}

and a lax limit encodes the data

x_{i}\in\Phi(i),i>j\leadsto\Phi_{ij}(x_{i})\xrightarrow{t_{ij}}x_{j}

compatible withe the data of
\displaystyle\Phi_{ij}
and
\displaystyle\eta_{ijk}
above. Here’s the formal definition:

Definition 9.0.1
.

A (right-)lax functor
\displaystyle\Phi:I\dashrightarrow\textnormal{Cat}
is a locally Cartesian fibration
\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{\Phi}
over
\displaystyle I^{\textnormal{op}}
. Its (left-)lax limit
\displaystyle\mathsf{Glue}(\Phi)
is the category of functors
\displaystyle\mathsf{sd}(I^{\textnormal{op}})^{\textnormal{op}}\to\mathcal{E}_{\Phi}
that preserve locally Cartesian
36
36

36

In Notation A.4.1 of
loc.cit.

Cartesian
arrows is written instead, but this is likely a typo.
arrows over
\displaystyle I^{\textnormal{op}}
, where
\displaystyle\mathsf{sd}
is the category of subdivisions defined in
loc.cit.

We also consider the oplax limit
\displaystyle\mathsf{opGlue}(\Psi)
of an oplax functor
\displaystyle\Psi
, defined analogously.

Convention 9.0.2
.

Our usage of “lax functor” refers to
right
-lax functors in
[
AMR21
]
, and “oplax functor” refers to
left
-lax functors; on the other hand, our usage of “lax limits” refer to their
left
-lax limits, and “oplax limits” refer to their
right
-lax limits. This sightly unfortunate hodgepodge is in alignment with the usage in
[
GR17
]
.
To maintain some sanity we will only speak of lax-limits of lax-functors and oplax-limits of oplax-functors; the other two combinations will not occur in this text.

.

It follows from
[

\displaystyle I

Remark 9.0.5
.

Let
\displaystyle\Phi,\Phi^{\prime}:I\dashrightarrow\textnormal{Cat}
be lax functors, and suppose we are given a fully faithful morphism
\displaystyle i:\Phi^{\prime}\to\Phi
, by which we mean a morphism
\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{\Phi^{\prime}}\to\mathcal{E}_{\Phi}
preserving locally Cartesian arrows, and which is a fiberwise fully faithful embedding of categories. Then we have an induced fully faithful embedding
\displaystyle\mathsf{Glue}(\Phi^{\prime})\subseteq\mathsf{Glue}(\Phi)
, whose essential image consists of those objects in
\displaystyle\mathfrak{G}(\Phi)
which lands in
\displaystyle\Phi^{\prime}
in each component.

We now summarize the main properties of lax limits:

Proposition 9.0.6
.

Let
\displaystyle\Phi:I\dashrightarrow\textnormal{Cat}
be a lax functor such that
\displaystyle\Phi(i)
all contain small colimits and
\displaystyle\Phi_{ij}
all commutes with small colimits. Let
\displaystyle I_{0}\subseteq I
a full subposet. Then the following hold:

1.

\displaystyle\mathsf{Glue}(\Phi)
contains small colimits, and the projection functor

The following general observation tells us that lax limits are ubiquitous in application:

Proposition 9.0.9
.

Let
\displaystyle C
be a category containing all small colimits,
\displaystyle\{C_{i}\}_{i\in I_{\textnormal{set}}}
a small set of cocomplete full subcategories. Let
\displaystyle F_{i}:C_{i}\to C
denote the inclusion functors, and suppose that their right adjoints
\displaystyle\{F_{i}^{R}\}
are continuous and jointly conservative. Let
\displaystyle I
be a poset whose underlying set of vertices is
\displaystyle I_{\textnormal{set}}
, such that for every
\displaystyle i\not\to j
in
\displaystyle I
, we have
\displaystyle F_{j}^{R}\circ F_{i}(\bullet)\simeq\textnormal{init}_{C_{j}}
. Then:

1.

The data
\displaystyle\Phi(i):=C_{i},\Phi_{ij}:=F_{j}^{R}\circ F_{i}
extends to a lax functor
\displaystyle\Phi:I\dashrightarrow\textnormal{Cat}
; and

2.

There exists an equivalence
\displaystyle\varphi:C\simeq\mathsf{Glue}(\Phi)
.

Proof.

We first build up
\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{\Phi}
by declaring it to be the full subcategory
\displaystyle\{(c,i)\in C\times I^{\textnormal{op}}\mid c\in C_{i}\}\subseteq C\times I^{\textnormal{op}}

Let

\displaystyle F_{i}
induce a oplax

Remark 10.1.2
.

This notion, as well as many others below, makes sense for both unital and non-unital operads. We do not dwell on this distinction too much, as it should always be clear from context which one is needed.

Definition 10.1.3
.

\displaystyle{\mathsf{Comm}_{\textnormal{nu}}}
is the nerve of the
\displaystyle(1,1)
-category consisting of nonempty finite sets and surjections among them.

Example 10.1.4
.

The
symmetric monoidal
envelope of the symmetric monoidal singleton category is the symmetric monoidal category
\displaystyle{\mathsf{Comm}_{\textnormal{nu}}}
. The symmetric monoidal envelope of
\displaystyle{\mathsf{Comm}_{\textnormal{nu}}}
is the twisted arrow category
\displaystyle\textnormal{Tw}({\mathsf{Comm}_{\textnormal{nu}}})^{\textnormal{op}}
.

Remark 10.1.5
.

It follows that a
commutative algebra object
in
\displaystyle\mathcal{C}^{\textnormal{corr}}
(which is a lax symmetric monoidal functor
\displaystyle*\to\mathcal{C}^{\textnormal{corr}}
) is also a symmetric monoidal functor
\displaystyle{\mathsf{Comm}_{\textnormal{nu}}}\to\mathcal{C}^{\textnormal{corr}}
, thus a composable symmetric monoidal functor
\displaystyle\textnormal{Tw}({\mathsf{Comm}_{\textnormal{nu}}})\to\mathcal{C}
, which is in turn an
oplax
functor
\displaystyle{\mathsf{Comm}_{\textnormal{nu}}}\to\mathcal{C}
satisfying some composability condition.

Monoidal Kan Extensions

We will need the following version of monoidal Kan extension, whose proof follows exactly that of
[
AFT16
, Lemma 2.16]
:

Lemma 10.1.6
.

Fix
\displaystyle\mathcal{O}^{\tensor}
an
\displaystyle\infty
-operad. Let
\displaystyle G:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
be an
\displaystyle\mathcal{O}^{\tensor}
-monoidal functor between
\displaystyle\mathcal{O}^{\tensor}
-monoidal categories such that
\displaystyle\mathcal{C}
is small and
\displaystyle\mathcal{D}
locally small. Suppose we have another
\displaystyle\mathcal{O}^{\tensor}
-monoidal category
\displaystyle\mathcal{V}
, and suppose there exists a subclass
\displaystyle\mathcal{K}
of
sSet
such that:

1.

\displaystyle\mathcal{V}
admits
\displaystyle\mathcal{K}
-limits;

2.

each slice category
\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{d/}
belongs to
\displaystyle\mathcal{K}
;

then the right Kan extension
\displaystyle\textnormal{RKE}_{F}:\textnormal{Fun}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{V})\to\textnormal{Fun}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{V})
exists. Furthermore, if

3.

for each active arrow
\displaystyle p:x\to y
in
\displaystyle\mathcal{O}^{\tensor}
and every
\displaystyle d\in\mathcal{D}^{(x)}
, the functor

\mathcal{C}^{(x)}_{d/}\to\mathcal{C}^{(y)}_{p(d)/}

is initial, where
\displaystyle d\to p(d)
is the coCartesian lift of
\displaystyle p
,

then the forgetful functors between the category of lax
\displaystyle\mathcal{O}^{\tensor}
-monoidal functors

\textnormal{Fun}^{\textnormal{lax},\mathcal{O}^{\tensor}}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{V})\to\textnormal{Fun}^{\textnormal{lax},\mathcal{O}^{\tensor}}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{V})

admits a right adjoint and is computed as right Kan extension of the underlying functor along
\displaystyle G
; finally, if further

4.

the
\displaystyle\mathcal{O}^{\tensor}
-monoidal structure of
\displaystyle\mathcal{V}
distributes over
\displaystyle\mathcal{K}
-limits;

then the right Kan extension also provides a right adjoint to the forgetful functors between the category of
\displaystyle\mathcal{O}^{\tensor}
-monoidal functors

\textnormal{Fun}^{\mathcal{O}^{\tensor}}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{V})\to\textnormal{Fun}^{\mathcal{O}^{\tensor}}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{V}).

An analogous statement holds true for left Kan extension as well.

Example 10.1.7
.

In the case of
\displaystyle\mathcal{O}^{\tensor}=\mathsf{Comm}
, the third condition is equivalent to the following:

•

The tensor product functor
\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{d_{1}/}\times\mathcal{C}_{d_{2}/}\to\mathcal{C}_{d_{1}\tensor d_{2}/}
is initial; and

•

The functor
\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\textbf{1}_{\mathcal{C}}/}\to\mathcal{C}_{\textbf{1}_{\mathcal{D}}/}
is initial.

10.2
Non-unital Factorization Spaces

For any given prestack
\displaystyle\mathcal{X}
, let
\displaystyle\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}(\mathcal{X})
denote the prestack associated with
\displaystyle\mathcal{X}
, defined as

\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu},\mathcal{X}}:=\colimit_{I\in({\mathsf{Comm}_{\textnormal{nu}}})^{\textnormal{op}}}\mathcal{X}^{I}

We let
\displaystyle[\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}]_{\textnormal{disj}}
to be the subfunctor whose
\displaystyle S
-point is given by

\{x:S\to X^{2},\alpha:S\times_{X^{2}}X\simeq\emptyset\};

then we let
\displaystyle[\mathcal{X}^{I}\times\mathcal{X}^{J}]_{\textnormal{disj}}
denote the subfunctor consisting of those points of
\displaystyle(\mathcal{X}^{I}\times\mathcal{X}^{J})(S)
such that for every
\displaystyle i\in I,j\in J
, the corresponding
\displaystyle S
-point of
\displaystyle\mathcal{X}^{2}
lies in
\displaystyle[\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{X}]_{\textnormal{disj}}
. Finally, we set

[\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu},\mathcal{X}}\times\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu},\mathcal{X}}]_{\textnormal{disj}}:=\colimit_{I,J\in({\mathsf{Comm}_{\textnormal{nu}}})^{\textnormal{op}}}[\mathcal{X}^{I}\times\mathcal{X}^{J}]_{\textnormal{disj}}.

Convention 10.2.1
.

We use
\displaystyle\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}
to denote
\displaystyle\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu},X}
(where
\displaystyle X
is our global curve) and
\displaystyle\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu},\textnormal{dR}}
for
\displaystyle\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu},X_{\textnormal{dR}}}
. When we use the latter, we refer to relevant objects as
crystals
of factorizable objects.

Definition 10.2.2
.

Let

\textnormal{WeakFactMonoid}_{\textnormal{nu}}:=\textnormal{Fun}^{\textnormal{oplax},\tensor}_{\textnormal{nu}}({\mathsf{Comm}_{\textnormal{nu}}},\textnormal{PreStk}).

An element of this category is called a non-unital
weak factorization monoids
.

Remark 10.2.3
.

For
\displaystyle\mathcal{C}
an arbitrary
\displaystyle(\infty,1)
-category, there is the
\displaystyle(\infty,1)
-category of correspondences in
\displaystyle\mathcal{C}
, defined in
[
Ras15
]
; we denote it by
\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\textnormal{corr}}
. By Remark
10.1.5
, a non-unital commutative algebra within
\displaystyle\textnormal{PreStk}_{\textnormal{corr}}
is a weak factorization space satisfying an extra
composability
condition. We will refer to such objects as
factorization monoids
.

Convention 10.2.4
.

When there is no ambiguity on the factorization structure, we will sometimes abuse notation and use the prestack
\displaystyle F([1])
to refer to the entire weak factorization monoid.

There are two non-unital factorization monoids whose underlying prestack is
\displaystyle\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}
. First the standard one, given by

\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}(I):=[\underbrace{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}\times\ldots\times\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}}_{|I|~\textnormal{times}}]_{\textnormal{disj}};

the oplax structure is the obvious inclusion
\displaystyle\iota
, and the map corresponding to
\displaystyle I\surj J
is the “add” map. In terms of correspondences, it can be depicted by the following diagram:

\displaystyle\textstyle{[\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}\times\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}]_{\textnormal{disj}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\iota}
\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\mathsf{add}}
\displaystyle\textstyle{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}\times\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}}
\displaystyle\textstyle{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}}

There is also
\displaystyle\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}^{\textnormal{comm}}
, the
commutative
Ran space, given by

\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}^{\textnormal{Comm}}(I):=\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}^{\times|I|}.

Graphically it is depicted as

\displaystyle\textstyle{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}\times\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
id
\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\mathsf{add}}
\displaystyle\textstyle{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}\times\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}}
\displaystyle\textstyle{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}}

Definition 10.2.5
.

We let
\displaystyle\textnormal{FactSpace}_{\textnormal{nu}}
denote the full subcategory of

\textnormal{Fun}^{\textnormal{oplax},\tensor}_{\textnormal{nu}}({\mathsf{Comm}_{\textnormal{nu}}},\textnormal{PreStk})_{/\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}}

consisting of oplax symmetric monoidal functors
\displaystyle F
over
\displaystyle\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}
satisfying the following conditions:

(Condition R)

Natural transformations as plain functors are Cartesian, i.e. we have the following Cartesian squares for all
\displaystyle I\surj J
:

\displaystyle\textstyle{F(I)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{F(J)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}(I)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}(J)}

(Condition L)

Natural transformations from the oplax structure are Cartesian, i.e. we have the following Cartesian squares for all
\displaystyle I\surj J
:

\displaystyle\textstyle{F(I)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{\prod_{j}F(I_{j})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}(I)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{\prod_{j}\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}(I_{j})}

An element of this category is referred to as a non-unital factorization space.

At the first level, condition R (resp. L) means that the right (resp. left) square of the following diagram is Cartesian:

\displaystyle\textstyle{F(2)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{F(1)\times F(1)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{[\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}\times\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}]_{\textnormal{disj}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{F(1)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}\times\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}}
\displaystyle\textstyle{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}}

10.2.6
Partition Description

Since the Ran space is a colimit over different
\displaystyle X^{I}
, we sometimes find it useful to describe factorization data as a collection of data living over
\displaystyle X^{I}
satisfying compatibilities. Here we follow the construction of
[
Ras15
, Section 8]
.

Notation 10.2.7
.

We set
\displaystyle\mathsf{Dbl}:=\textnormal{Tw}({\mathsf{Comm}_{\textnormal{nu}}})^{\textnormal{op}}
and
\displaystyle\mathsf{Tpl}:=\textnormal{Env}(\mathsf{Dbl})
.

Definition 10.2.8
.

Introduce
\displaystyle U_{\textnormal{Ran}}\in\textnormal{Fun}^{\textnormal{oplax},\tensor}_{\textnormal{nu}}(\mathsf{Dbl}^{\textnormal{op}},\textnormal{PreStk})
such that

U_{\textnormal{Ran}}(p:I\surj J)(S):=\{(x_{i})_{i\in I}\in X^{I}(S)\mid p(i_{1})\neq p(i_{2})\implies x_{i_{1}}\neq x_{i_{2}}~\forall i_{1},i_{2}\in I\}

This is the “partition” incarnation of the Ran space; it is again an oplax symmetric monoidal functor.

Let
\displaystyle\pi:\mathsf{Dbl}^{\textnormal{op}}\to{\mathsf{Comm}_{\textnormal{nu}}},(I\surj J)\mapsto J
denote the projection. Operadic left Kan extension (Lemma
10.1.6
) preserves oplax symmetric monoidal functors, and we observe that
\displaystyle\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}\simeq\textnormal{LKE}_{\pi}(U_{\textnormal{Ran}})
because
\displaystyle\pi
is a coCartesian fibration.

Definition 10.2.9
.

We let
\displaystyle\textnormal{FactSpace}_{\textnormal{nu},\textnormal{Part}}
denote the full subcategory of
\displaystyle\textnormal{Fun}^{\textnormal{oplax},\tensor}_{\textnormal{nu}}(\mathsf{Dbl}^{\textnormal{op}},\textnormal{PreStk})_{/U_{\textnormal{Ran}}}
consisting of functors
\displaystyle F
over
\displaystyle U_{\textnormal{Ran}}
such that:

(Condition R’)

Natural transformations as plain functors are Cartesian, i.e. we have the following Cartesian squares for all
\displaystyle(I^{\prime}\to J^{\prime})\to(I\to J)\in\mathsf{Dbl}
:

\displaystyle\textstyle{F(I\surj J)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{F(I^{\prime}\surj J^{\prime})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{U_{\textnormal{Ran}}(I\surj J)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{U_{\textnormal{Ran}}(I^{\prime}\surj J^{\prime})}

(Condition L’)

Natural transformations from the oplax structure are Cartesian, i.e. we have the following Cartesian squares for all
\displaystyle I\surj J\surj K
:

\displaystyle\textstyle{F(I\surj J)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{\prod_{k}F(I_{k}\surj J_{k})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{U_{\textnormal{Ran}}(I\surj J)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{\prod_{k}U_{\textnormal{Ran}}(I_{k}\surj J_{k})}

The following fact is parallel to
[
Ras15
, Section 8]

Proposition 10.2.10
.

\displaystyle\textnormal{FactSpace}_{\textnormal{nu}}\simeq\textnormal{FactSpace}_{\textnormal{nu},\textnormal{Part}}
.

Modulo a quick combinatorial check, this reduces to a general claim about left Kan extensions described below, to which we devote the rest of this subsection. Since the proof is pure combinatorics, we recommend skipping it on the first pass.

Definition 10.2.11
.

For a cospan
\displaystyle I\surj^{p}J^{\prime}\twoheadleftarrow^{q}J
in
\displaystyle{\mathsf{Comm}_{\textnormal{nu}}}
, define the (ordinary) category
\displaystyle\textnormal{Factor}(p,q)
:

•

Its objects are surjections
\displaystyle I\surj^{r}J
such that
\displaystyle q\circ r=p
; and

•

A map
\displaystyle r\to r^{\prime}
is a bijection
\displaystyle a:I\simeq I
such that
\displaystyle r\circ a=r^{\prime}
,
\displaystyle p\circ a=p
.

when the relevant maps are clear sometimes we just write
\displaystyle\textnormal{Factor}(I\surj J^{\prime}\twoheadleftarrow J)
.

Proposition 10.2.12
.

Suppose
\displaystyle\mathcal{C}
is a symmetric monoidal
\displaystyle\infty
-topos, such that the monoidal product commutes with filtered colimits in each variable and distributes over pullbacks. Let
\displaystyle U:\mathsf{Dbl}^{\textnormal{op}}\to\mathcal{C}
be a oplax symmetric monoidal functor, and
\displaystyle\textnormal{LKE}_{\pi}(U):{\mathsf{Comm}_{\textnormal{nu}}}\to\mathcal{C}
be its (operadic) left Kan extension. Suppose that, for every diagram

\displaystyle\textstyle{E\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{B\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{C\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{D}

in
\displaystyle{\mathsf{Comm}_{\textnormal{nu}}}
, the outer square (equivalently, both squares) of the diagram

\displaystyle\textstyle{\colimit_{\textnormal{Factor}(B\surj C\twoheadleftarrow E)}U(B\surj E)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{\colimit_{\textnormal{Factor}(A\surj C\twoheadleftarrow E)}U(A\surj E)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{U(B\surj C)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{U(A\surj C)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{\bigotimes_{d\in D}U(B_{d}\surj C_{d})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{\bigotimes_{d\in D}U(A_{d}\surj C_{d})}

is Cartesian. Then operadic Kan extension

\textnormal{LKE}_{\pi}^{/U}:\textnormal{Fun}^{\textnormal{oplax},\tensor}_{\textnormal{nu}}(\mathsf{Dbl}^{\textnormal{op}},\mathcal{C})_{/U}\to\textnormal{Fun}^{\textnormal{oplax},\tensor}_{\textnormal{nu}}({\mathsf{Comm}_{\textnormal{nu}}},\mathcal{C})_{/\textnormal{LKE}_{\pi}(U)}

induces an equivalence between the full subcategory of LHS satisfying condition (R’) and (L’) as in Definition
10.2.9
and the full subcategory of RHS satisfying condition (R) and (L) as in Definition
10.2.5
.

Proof.

Note that
\displaystyle\mathsf{Dbl}
is the comonoidal envelope of
\displaystyle{\mathsf{Comm}_{\textnormal{nu}}}
and
\displaystyle\mathsf{Tpl}^{\textnormal{op}}
is the comonoidal envelope of
\displaystyle\mathsf{Dbl}^{\textnormal{op}}
. Then there is a commutative diagram

\displaystyle\textstyle{\textnormal{Fun}^{\textnormal{oplax},\tensor}_{\textnormal{nu}}(\mathsf{Dbl}^{\textnormal{op}},\mathcal{C})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\textnormal{LKE}_{\pi}}
\displaystyle\scriptstyle{F\mapsto F_{\textnormal{univ}}}
\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\simeq}
\displaystyle\textstyle{\textnormal{Fun}^{\textnormal{oplax},\tensor}_{\textnormal{nu}}({\mathsf{Comm}_{\textnormal{nu}}},\mathcal{C})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\scriptstyle{F\mapsto F_{\textnormal{univ}}}
\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\simeq}
Res
\displaystyle\textstyle{\textnormal{Fun}^{\tensor}(\mathsf{Tpl}^{\textnormal{op}},\mathcal{C})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\scriptstyle{\textnormal{LKE}_{\tau}}
\displaystyle\textstyle{\textnormal{Fun}^{\tensor}(\mathsf{Dbl},\mathcal{C})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
Res

where
\displaystyle\tau(I\surj J\surj K)=(J\surj K)
; note that
\displaystyle\textnormal{LKE}_{\tau}
is again just computed by LKE on the underlying functor. Let

\mathcal{L}:=\textnormal{LKE}_{\tau}^{/U_{\textnormal{univ}}}:\textnormal{Fun}^{\tensor}(\mathsf{Tpl}^{\textnormal{op}},\mathcal{C})_{/U_{\textnormal{univ}}}\to\textnormal{Fun}^{\tensor}(\mathsf{Dbl},\mathcal{C})_{/\textnormal{LKE}_{\tau}(U_{\textnormal{univ}})}

be the induced functor; its right adjoint
\displaystyle\mathcal{R}
is then given by sending
\displaystyle F_{\textnormal{univ}}
to the fiber product

U_{\textnormal{univ}}\times_{\textnormal{Res}\circ\textnormal{LKE}_{\tau}(U_{\textnormal{univ}})}\textnormal{Res}(F_{\textnormal{univ}})

within the category
\displaystyle\textnormal{Fun}^{\tensor}(\mathsf{Tpl}^{\textnormal{op}},\mathcal{C})
. Since the category of symmetric monoidal functors embed fully faithfully into the category of
lax
symmetric monoidal functor, i.e. commutative algebra objects in the Day convolution monoidal structure, and because tensor product distributes over pullbacks by assumption, this pullback can be computed in the underlying category

\displaystyle\textnormal{Fun}(\mathsf{Tpl}^{\textnormal{op}},\mathcal{C})
.

For brevity, set
\displaystyle R:=\textnormal{LKE}_{\pi}(U)
, so that
\displaystyle R_{\textnormal{univ}}\simeq\textnormal{LKE}_{\tau}(U_{\textnormal{univ}})
. We let

•

\displaystyle\mathscr{L}
denote the full subcategory of
\displaystyle\textnormal{Fun}^{\tensor}(\mathsf{Tpl}^{\textnormal{op}},\mathcal{C})_{/U_{\textnormal{univ}}}
consisting of those object
\displaystyle G_{\textnormal{univ}}
such that, for every
\displaystyle(I\surj J\surj K)\to(I^{\prime}\surj J^{\prime}\surj K^{\prime})
in
\displaystyle\mathsf{Tpl}^{\textnormal{op}}
, the following square is Cartesian:

\displaystyle\textstyle{G_{\textnormal{univ}}(I\surj J\surj K)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{G_{\textnormal{univ}}(I^{\prime}\surj J^{\prime}\surj K^{\prime})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{\bigotimes_{k}U(I_{k}\surj J_{k})\simeq U_{\textnormal{univ}}(I\surj J\surj K)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{U_{\textnormal{univ}}(I^{\prime}\surj J^{\prime}\surj K^{\prime})\simeq\bigotimes_{k^{\prime}}U(I^{\prime}_{k^{\prime}}\surj J^{\prime}_{k^{\prime}})}

•

\displaystyle\mathscr{R}
denote the full subcategory of
\displaystyle\textnormal{Fun}^{\tensor}(\mathsf{Dbl},\mathcal{C})_{/R_{\textnormal{univ}}}
consisting of those object
\displaystyle F_{\textnormal{univ}}
such that, for every
\displaystyle(J\surj K)\to(J^{\prime}\surj K^{\prime})
in
\displaystyle\mathsf{Dbl}
, the following square is Cartesian:

\displaystyle\textstyle{F_{\textnormal{univ}}(J\surj K)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{F_{\textnormal{univ}}(J^{\prime}\surj K^{\prime})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{\bigotimes_{k}R(J_{k})\simeq R_{\textnormal{univ}}(J\surj K)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{R_{\textnormal{univ}}(J^{\prime}\surj K^{\prime})\simeq\bigotimes_{k^{\prime}}R(J^{\prime}_{k^{\prime}})}

It is immediate that the two subcategories originally considered correspond to
\displaystyle\mathscr{L}
and
\displaystyle\mathscr{R}
respectively. Our job then is to check that

and
\displaystyle\textnormal{LKE}_{\tau}
both preserve these subcategories, and on these subcategories the unit/counit induce isomorphisms on the level of underlying functors.

If
\displaystyle F_{\textnormal{univ}}\in\mathscr{R}
then
\displaystyle\mathcal{R}(F_{\textnormal{univ}})\in\mathscr{L}
by unfolding definition. Conversely, for

by cofinality, so our job is to prove, for any fixed map

is Cartesian, where

to

\displaystyle\textstyle{\colimit_{a\in\mathcal{A}}U_{\textnormal{univ}}(a\surj J^{\prime}\surj K^{\prime})}

We claim that this is the same as the colimit of pullbacks

\colimit_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern Assuming this, since colimits are universal, we can write the pullback as

\colimit_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\colimit_{b\in\mathcal{B}_{a}}\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern \simeq\colimit_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\colimit_{b\in\mathcal{B}_{a}}G_{\textnormal{univ}}(b\surj J\surj K)\simeq\colimit_{\mathcal{B}}G_{\textnormal{univ}}

as desired. To check the claim, rewrite

x_{a}=G_{\textnormal{univ}}(a\surj J^{\prime}\surj K^{\prime}),y_{a}=U_{\textnormal{univ}}(a\surj J^{\prime}\surj K^{\prime}),z_{a}=\colimit_{b\in\mathcal{B}_{a}}U_{\textnormal{univ}}(b\surj J\surj K);

x=\colimit_{a}x_{a},y=\colimit_{a}y_{a},z=\colimit_{a}z_{a}.

The claim is that
\displaystyle\colimit_{a}x_{a}\times_{y_{a}}z_{a}\simeq x\times_{y}z
. Since colimits are universal, we always have
\displaystyle x\times_{y}z\simeq\colimit_{a}x_{a}\times_{y}z\simeq\colimit_{a}x_{a}\times_{y_{a}}y_{a}\times_{y}z
, so we only need
\displaystyle y_{a}\times_{y}z\simeq z_{a}
, i.e. we need for every fixed
\displaystyle I^{\prime}\surj J^{\prime}
, the diagram

\displaystyle\textstyle{\colimit_{\textnormal{Factor}(I^{\prime}\surj J^{\prime}\twoheadleftarrow J)}U_{\textnormal{univ}}(I^{\prime}\surj J\surj K)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{\textnormal{LKE}_{\tau}U_{\textnormal{univ}}(J\surj K)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{\bigotimes_{k^{\prime}\in K^{\prime}}U(I^{\prime}_{k^{\prime}}\surj J^{\prime}_{k^{\prime}})\simeq U_{\textnormal{univ}}(I^{\prime}\surj J^{\prime}\surj K^{\prime})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{\textnormal{LKE}_{\tau}U_{\textnormal{univ}}(J^{\prime}\surj K^{\prime})\simeq\bigotimes_{k^{\prime}\in K^{\prime}}\textnormal{LKE}_{\pi}U(J^{\prime}_{k^{\prime}})}

One further reduces to
\displaystyle|K|=1
; this then follows from descent and our assumption on
\displaystyle U
.

Universality of colimits guarantees
\displaystyle\mathcal{L}\circ\mathcal{R}\simeq\textnormal{id}
; to check
\displaystyle\textnormal{id}\simeq\mathcal{R}\circ\mathcal{L}
on
\displaystyle\mathscr{L}
, note that we have a pullback square

\displaystyle\textstyle{\mathcal{R}\circ\mathcal{L}(G_{\textnormal{univ}})(I\surj J\surj K)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{\colimit_{I^{\prime}\surj J}G_{\textnormal{univ}}(I^{\prime}\surj J\surj K)\simeq\textnormal{Res}\circ\textnormal{LKE}_{\tau}(G_{\textnormal{univ}})(I\surj J\surj K)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{U_{\textnormal{univ}}(I\surj J\surj K)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{\colimit_{I^{\prime}\surj J}U_{\textnormal{univ}}(I^{\prime}\surj J\surj K)\simeq\textnormal{Res}\circ\textnormal{LKE}_{\tau}(U_{\textnormal{univ}})(I\surj J\surj K)}

Descent and the condition on
\displaystyle\mathscr{L}
then guarantees that the pullback is isomorphic to
\displaystyle G_{\textnormal{univ}}(I\surj J\surj K)
.
∎

10.3
Unital Factorization Spaces

Now we introduce the unital Ran space
\displaystyle\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{un}}
.

Definition 10.3.1
.

The
unital
Ran space
\displaystyle\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{un}}
is the lax prestack whose
\displaystyle S
-point is the poset category of (potentially empty) finite subsets of
\displaystyle X(S)
with the inclusion relation.

As we can write
\displaystyle\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}=\colimit_{I\in{\mathsf{Comm}_{\textnormal{nu}}}^{\textnormal{op}}}X^{I}
, we can also write the unital Ran as a
partially oplax colimit
.

Definition 10.3.2
.

Let
\displaystyle F:C\to 1\textnormal{-Cat}
be a functor, and
\displaystyle I
be a class of morphisms in
\displaystyle C
. Let
\displaystyle\textnormal{Cart}(F)\to C^{\textnormal{op}}
be the corresponding Cartesian fibration. The partially oplax colimit, which we denote by
\displaystyle\textnormal{oplax}\colimit_{C,I}F
, is the localization of
\displaystyle\textnormal{Cart}(F)
with respect to all Cartesian arrows that lies above arrows in
\displaystyle I
.

Definition 10.3.3
.

Let
\displaystyle\mathsf{Comm}
denote the category of all (potentially empty) finite sets and arbitrary morphisms among them; it contains
\displaystyle{\mathsf{Comm}_{\textnormal{nu}}}
as a 1-full subcategory.

Let
\displaystyle X^{(-)}
denote the functor
\displaystyle\mathsf{Comm}^{\textnormal{op}}\to\textnormal{PreStk}
; it follows from unpacking definition (c.f.
[
Gai19
]
) that

\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{un}}\simeq\textnormal{oplax}\colimit_{\mathsf{Comm}^{\textnormal{op}},{\mathsf{Comm}_{\textnormal{nu}}}^{\textnormal{op}}}X^{(-)}.

Definition 10.3.4
.

An
unital
weak factorization monoid is an
oplax

oplax-unital

41

41

This means that for such a monoid
\displaystyle F
,
\displaystyle F(0)
is
not

.
symmetric monoidal functor from
\displaystyle\mathsf{Comm}
to

; the category is denoted as

\textnormal{WeakFactMonoid}_{\textnormal{un}}:=\textnormal{Fun}^{\textnormal{oplax},\tensor}(\mathsf{Comm},\textnormal{LaxPreStk}).

We have the following correspondence diagram:

\displaystyle\textstyle{[\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{un}}\times\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{un}}]_{\textnormal{disj}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}
\displaystyle\textstyle{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{un}}\times\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{un}}}
\displaystyle\textstyle{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{un}}}

\displaystyle\textstyle{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{un}}}

\displaystyle[\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{un}}\times\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{un}}]_{\textnormal{disj}}

consisting of objects that lies in
\displaystyle[\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}\times\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}]_{\textnormal{disj}}

\displaystyle\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{un}}
.

Definition 10.3.5
.

We let
\displaystyle\textnormal{FactSpace}_{\textnormal{un}}
denote the 1-full subcategory of

(Condition R)

Natural transformations as plain functors are Cartesian for

\displaystyle\textstyle{F(I)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}

(Condition L)

Natural transformations from the oplax structure are Cartesian for

\displaystyle\textstyle{F(I)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}

(Condition F)

For each

42

42

In the model-independent world, “left fibration” means “coCartesian fibration fibered in spaces”.
(i.e. it is pointwise a left fibration in a functorial way);

(Condition P)

A map
\displaystyle F\Rightarrow G
between two elements is required to pointwise preserve coCartesian arrows;

(Condition C)

For every composable pair of morphisms
\displaystyle I\to J\to K
in
\displaystyle\mathsf{Comm}

\displaystyle\textstyle{\prod_{k=1}^{K}F(I_{k})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces}

\displaystyle\textstyle{\prod_{j=1}^{J}F([1])}

is Cartesian.

A unital factorization space is then an element of
\displaystyle\textnormal{FactSpace}_{\textnormal{un}}
.

Remark 10.3.6
.

Condition C corresponds to composability in Lemma
10.1.1
; it was redundant in the non-unital case because it is implied by condition R and L, and the fact that
\displaystyle\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{nu}}
itself satisfies condition C.

Variant 10.3.7
.

We let
\displaystyle\textnormal{FactSpace}_{\textnormal{un},\textnormal{weak}}
denote the category sharing the same definition as above but with condition (R) dropped. An element of this category is referred to as a
weak
unital factorization space.

Variant 10.3.8
.

If we drop condition P above, we obtain the notion of a
lax-unital
morphism between factorization spaces. The category of factorization spaces and lax-unital morphisms between them is denoted
\displaystyle[\textnormal{FactSpace}_{\textnormal{un}}]_{\textnormal{lax-unital}}
.

Variant 10.3.9
.

If we replace “left” in condition F by “right” and “coCartesian” in condition P by “Cartesian”, we obtain the notion of a
co-unital
factorization space (the category of which is denoted
\displaystyle\textnormal{FactSpace}_{\textnormal{co-un}}
). The lax-counital version is denoted
\displaystyle[\textnormal{FactSpace}_{\textnormal{co-un}}]_{\textnormal{lax-counital}}
.

Let us explain how this definition compare with the existing definitions in literature.
For every map
\displaystyle\varphi:S\to\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{un}}
from an arbitrary prestack
\displaystyle S
, let
\displaystyle C_{\varphi}
denote the fiber product lax prestack; since condition F requires the fibration to be fibered in spaces,
\displaystyle C_{\varphi}
will be an actual prestack.
The coCartesian part of condition F implies that, for every natural transformation
\displaystyle\varphi\Rightarrow\psi:S\to\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{un}}
, we have a map
\displaystyle C_{\varphi}\to C_{\psi}
as prestacks over
\displaystyle S
. Condition P further guarantees that this construction is functorial in
\displaystyle S
, and thus combines into a map

\textnormal{Fun}([1],\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{un}})\times_{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{un}},\textnormal{source}}F(\textbf{1})\to F(\textbf{1})

which is the structured described in e.g.
[
Gai17a
, Section 4]
.
In particular, for an injective map
\displaystyle I\inj J
, the natural transformation

(X^{J}\to X^{I}\to\textnormal{Ran}\to\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{un}})\Rightarrow(X^{J}\to\textnormal{Ran}\to\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{un}})

gives a morphism

X^{J}\times_{X^{I}}(F(\textbf{1})\times_{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{un}}}X^{I})\to(F(\textbf{1})\times_{\textnormal{Ran}_{\textnormal{un}}}X^{J})

which is the usual unital data.

The following definition is reminiscent of the “relative”
\displaystyle\infty
-category theory developed in
[
Sha17
]
:

Definition 10.3.10
.

Let
\displaystyle C_{1}\xrightarrow{\varphi}C_{2}\xrightarrow{\pi}D
be maps between simplicial sets, such that
\displaystyle\pi\circ\varphi
and
\displaystyle\pi
are both flat inner fibrations. We say
\displaystyle\varphi
has
\displaystyle D
-left anodyne lifting property if, for every map
\displaystyle A\xrightarrow{i}B\xrightarrow{p}D
where
\displaystyle i
is left anodyne, the induced map

(C_{1}^{B}\times_{D^{B}}\{p\})\to(C_{1}^{A}\times_{D^{A}}\{p\circ i\})\times_{(C_{2}^{A}\times_{D^{A}}\{p\circ i\})}(C_{2}^{B}\times_{D^{B}}\{p\})

is a trivial Kan fibration. The notion of
\displaystyle D
-right anodyne lifting property is defined analogously.

Example 10.3.11
.

By
[
Lur09
, 2.1.2.9]
if
\displaystyle\varphi
is itself a left/right fibration, then it has
\displaystyle D
-left/right anodyne lifting property for any
\displaystyle D
.

Variant 10.3.12
.

We can further weaken condition F to being a
flat inner fibration

In the corr-unital case, we have four types of condition P:

1.

The default notion is when we drop condition P altogether. The resulting category will be denoted
\displaystyle\textnormal{FactSpace}_{\textnormal{corr-un}}

2.

We can restrict morphism spaces to those maps

\displaystyle[\textnormal{FactSpace}_{\textnormal{corr-un}}]_{\textnormal{str-unital}}

We can replace “left” with “right” above and obtain a dual version of corr-unital factorization spaces

\displaystyle[\textnormal{FactSpace}_{\textnormal{corr-un}}]_{\textnormal{str-counital}}
